title: 1941: Counter Attack
blurb: Capcom's vertical shooter sends you skyward in February 1990, with a high-score quirk only export cabinets share.
about: 1941 - Counter Attack is a Capcom arcade shooter that reached players outside Japan in February 1990. It runs on the CP System hardware. Export versions carry a small difference from the Japanese original: the fifth spot on the high score table reads 'a02' rather than 'j01'. The board is identified as B-Board 89624B-3.

title: Cadillacs and Dinosaurs
blurb: Cadillacs and Dinosaurs pits street brawlers against prehistoric beasts in Capcom's 1993 arcade hit.
about: Cadillacs and Dinosaurs is a Capcom arcade game released in February 1993 outside Japan, where it was known as Cadillacs Kyouryuu Shin Seiki, or Cadillacs New Dinosaur Century. This export version runs on Capcom Play System hardware with a B-Board numbered 91635B-2. One difference from the Japanese original: the scrolling text effect during the storyline was removed from all export releases.
tips: Up to three players can fight together as Jack, Hannah, Mustapha or Mess.
Guns dropped by enemies have limited ammo; when one runs dry, your fighter throws it away and goes back to fists.
One stage puts you behind the wheel of the Cadillac, where you run down enemies on the road.

title: Captain Commando
blurb: Capcom's 1991 arcade brawler arrives in an export version with renamed heroes Ginzu, Mack the Knife, and Baby Head.
about: Captain Commando is a 1991 Capcom arcade release, developed in Japan and issued as an export version on B-Board 91635B-2. In this export release, Sho is called Ginzu, Jennety is called Mack the Knife, and Hoover is called Baby Head.

title: Carrier Air Wing
blurb: Capcom's 1990 arcade shooter flies as an export release with one notable graphical change from the Japanese version.
about: Carrier Airwing is a 1990 Capcom arcade release, developed in Japan and issued as an export version on CP System hardware with B-Board ID 89624B-3. A character resembling Sean Connery looks even more like him in the Japanese release than in the export versions, where the graphic was changed — perhaps to avoid license issues in the U.S.

title: Dynasty Wars
blurb: Capcom's 1989 arcade brawler Dynasty Wars brings ancient Chinese warfare to the coin-op screen.
about: Dynasty Wars is a Capcom arcade game released in July 1989 outside Japan, where it was titled Tenchi wo Kurau, translating to Heaven and Earth Receiving Blows. This export version runs on CP System hardware with a B-Board ID of 88622B-3.

title: Final Fight
blurb: Capcom's 1990 arcade brawler cleans up the streets with fists and fury.
about: Final Fight is a Capcom arcade beat'em up released in 1990. This export version was developed in Japan and runs on CP System hardware with B-Board ID 89624B-3. The original Japanese release included a scene showing Jessica in underwear on a TV in abstract mode, which was removed from all export versions. Completing the game on a single credit unlocks a special credits screen.

title: Knights of the Round
blurb: Capcom's 1991 arcade hack-and-slash lets you become a knight of the round table.
about: This is the export version of Capcom's 1991 arcade beat 'em up, Knights of the Round. It is a side-scrolling action game based on the legends of King Arthur and his knights. For more information about the game itself, please see the original Japanese release entry. It runs on the CP System hardware.

title: Magic Sword
blurb: Capcom's 1990 CPS1 export release of Magic Sword brings its heroic fantasy arcade action to Western players.
about: Magic Sword - Heroic Fantasy is an arcade game released by Capcom in 1990, running on CP System hardware. This entry is the export version of a title developed in Japan.

title: Mega Twins
blurb: Capcom's 1990 CPS1 export release of Mega Twins delivers the arcade action of Chiki Chiki Boys overseas.
about: Mega Twins is an arcade game released by Capcom in 1990, running on CP System hardware. This export version was developed in Japan, and the kidnapped bikini girls seen in later levels of the original are absent.

title: Muscle Bomber Duo: Ultimate Team Battle
saveName: Muscle Bomber Duo: Ultimate Team Battle
blurb: Capcom's 1993 wrestling tag battle brings team-based slamdowns to the arcade.
about: Muscle Bomber Duo - Ultimate Team Battle is Capcom's 1993 export release of the tag-team wrestling fighter, running on Capcom Play System hardware. For non-Japanese audiences, several wrestlers were renamed: Zalazoff became Biff Slamkovich, Colt became Gunloc, Budo became Oni, Stinger became El Stingray, Sheep became Alexander The Grater, Gomes became Rasta, Kimala became Jumbo, and Astro became Scorpion.

title: Pang! 3
blurb: Mitchell's bubble-bursting arcade series returns for a third round of frantic action.
about: Pang! 3 is Mitchell's 1995 arcade release, developed in Japan and distributed as an export title. For full details on the game itself, see the original Japanese entry, Pang! 3 - Kaitou Tachi no Karei na Gogo. North American players know the game as Buster Buddies. The official record for it belongs to Sheila Van Buren, with 2,256,411 points.

title: Pnickies
blurb: Capcom and Compile's colorful puzzle game brings blob-matching action to arcades.
about: Pnickies is a puzzle game released by Capcom in June 1994 for Japanese arcades. Up to two players can compete simultaneously using an 8-way joystick and two buttons each. It was developed by Compile and was known as the 29th video game made for the CP System hardware.

title: Street Fighter II': Champion Edition
blurb: The 1992 arcade export edition of Street Fighter II' Champion Edition from Capcom, running on CPS-1 hardware.
about: Street Fighter II' - Champion Edition is a 1992 Capcom arcade fighting game released as an export version and developed in Japan. It runs on Capcom Play System hardware, with the B-Board numbered 91635B-2. This export release is tied to the original Japanese version, Street Fighter II' - Champion Edition [B-Board 91634B-2], for full details about the game itself.
tips: Champion Edition was the first version of Street Fighter II in which the four bosses (Balrog, Vega, Sagat and M. Bison) can be picked, and the first to allow both players to choose the same fighter.
Ryu and Ken: the Hadoken is down, down-forward, forward + punch, and the Shoryuken is forward, down, down-forward + punch.
Charge fighters (Guile, Blanka, E. Honda, Chun-Li, Balrog, Vega, M. Bison) hold back or down for about two seconds before the release motion.

title: Street Fighter II': Hyper Fighting
blurb: Capcom's 1992 export arcade fighter Street Fighter II' Hyper Fighting, built on CPS-1 hardware.
about: Street Fighter II' - Hyper Fighting is a 1992 Capcom arcade fighting game released as an export version and developed in Japan. It runs on Capcom Play System hardware, with the B-Board numbered 91635B-2. Outside Japan it arrived in December 1992, while in Japan the same game is known as Street Fighter II' Turbo - Hyper Fighting. For details about the game itself, see the original Japanese release entry.
tips: Hyper Fighting is the faster revision of Champion Edition: all twelve fighters can be picked, the four bosses included, and the whole game runs at a higher speed.

Ryu and Ken share the core special moves: the Hadoken fireball is down, down-forward, forward + punch, the Shoryuken uppercut is forward, down, down-forward + punch, and the Hurricane Kick is down, down-back, back + kick.

Guile, Blanka, E. Honda, Chun-Li, Balrog, Vega and M. Bison use charge moves: hold back (or down) for about two seconds, then press the opposite direction with an attack, for example back, then forward + punch for Guile's Sonic Boom.
Throw when you are right next to your opponent: hold toward or away and press a medium or heavy punch.

title: The King of Dragons
blurb: Capcom's 1991 fantasy beat-'em-up lets you battle dragons and monsters as five distinct hero classes.
about: The King of Dragons is a 1991 Capcom arcade beat-'em-up released on CPS1 hardware. Players pick from character classes including Fighter, Cleric, and Wizard, each leveling up and gaining new abilities as they fight through a fantasy world of orcs, lizardmen, and dragons. This B-Board 89625B-1 revision differs notably from the earlier World version: the Cleric starts with 40 HP instead of 48, the first extra life arrives at 200,000 points rather than 100,000, fruit restores only 12 HP, and new foes like green lizard spearmen appear. It uses a single 4-Mbit EPROM instead of four 1-Mbit chips.

title: Three Wonders
blurb: Capcom's three-in-one 1991 arcade package, with export tweaks to the action chapter.
about: Three Wonders is a Capcom arcade release from 1991, running on the CP System hardware with B-Board 89624B-3. It was developed in Japan and saw export releases. Export versions differ from the Japanese original: the action game is titled 'Midnight Wanderers' instead of 'Roosters', and it plays slightly easier, with the stage 1 mid-boss firing at a lower rate and the stage 1 end-boss shooting more while punching less.

title: U.N. Squadron
blurb: Capcom's 1989 arcade shooter soars into North American arcades with intense aerial combat.
about: U.N. Squadron is Capcom USA's North American arcade release from August 1989, known in Japan as Area 88. It is a side-scrolling shoot-'em-up. This version notably omits the special mission found in the Japanese original. It runs on Capcom Play System hardware.

title: Varth: Operation Thunderstorm
blurb: Capcom's 1992 vertical shooter deploys worldwide for relentless arcade aerial warfare.
about: Varth: Operation Thunderstorm is Capcom's 1992 export release of the Japanese-developed arcade shooter. It runs on CP System hardware. For full gameplay details, refer to the original Japanese release entry.

title: Warriors of Fate
blurb: Capcom's 1992 beat 'em up Warriors of Fate brings Three Kingdoms combat to arcades worldwide.
about: Warriors of Fate is a 1992 Capcom Company, Limited arcade game released worldwide on CP System hardware, developed in Japan and known there as Tenchi wo Kurau II - Sekiheki no Tatakai and in Asia as Sangokushi II. It runs on a B-Board 91635B-2. Released in October 1992, the export version trims many scenes from the Japanese original: cutscenes with the third emperor, advisor messages, boss dialogues across stages, and a long stage 5 scene with a woman and baby. In-game names lost their kanji and were changed without proper translation.

title: Willow
blurb: Capcom USA's 1989 arcade release Willow arrives on CP System hardware for export regions.
about: Willow is a 1989 Capcom USA, Incorporated arcade video game released for export territories and developed in Japan. It runs on the CP System hardware with B-Board ID 89624B-3.

title: 1944: The Loop Master
blurb: Capcom's CPS-II aerial shooter landed in the USA on June 20, 2000, and it runs on the blue board.
about: 1944 - The Loop Master is a Capcom arcade shooter built for the CP System II hardware, arriving in North America on June 20, 2000. The game was developed in Japan. The USA release uses the blue board configuration.

title: 19XX: The War Against Destiny
blurb: Capcom's 1996 CPS-II shooter reached North America and Europe on the blue board hardware.
about: 19XX - The War Against Destiny is a Capcom arcade shooter released in 1996 for the CP System II hardware. It saw a North American and European release, with development handled in Japan. The overseas version runs on the blue board configuration.

title: Alien vs. Predator
blurb: Capcom's 1994 CPS-II crossover pits the galaxy's deadliest hunters against its deadliest prey.
about: Alien vs. Predator is an arcade game released by Capcom USA, Incorporated in 1994 on CP System II hardware, in North American and European release. It was developed in Japan. This Blue Board edition followed the original Japanese release, Alien vs. Predator, which arrived on a Green Board.

title: Armored Warriors
blurb: Capcom's 1994 CPS-II mech brawler, released in North America and Europe after its Japanese debut.
about: Armored Warriors is an arcade game released by Capcom Company, Limited in 1994 on CP System II hardware, in North American and European release. It was developed in Japan. This Blue Board edition followed the original Japanese release, Powered Gear - Strategic Variant Armor Equipment, which arrived on a Green Board.

title: Battle Circuit
blurb: Capcom's 1997 CPS-II brawler arrived in Europe as a blue-board release.
about: Battle Circuit is a Capcom arcade beat-'em-up that ran on CP System II hardware. The version covered here is the European blue-board release. Developed in Japan in 1997, it reached Europe under Capcom Company, Limited. A separate original Japanese green-board release also exists.

title: Capcom Sports Club
blurb: Capcom's sports mini-game collection arrives on CPS-II hardware in this European release.
about: Capcom Sports Club is a Capcom CPS-II arcade title released in 1997, developed in Japan and published in Europe on Blue Board hardware.

title: Cyberbots: Fullmetal Madness
blurb: Pilot massive mechs into combat in Capcom's 2D fighting game of armored duels.
about: Cyberbots - Fullmetal Madness is a Capcom CPS-II arcade fighting game released in 1995, developed in Japan and published across North America and Europe. The export versions differ from the Japanese original: the Vs. screen drops the chapter titles and VA model numbers, victory quotes lose their voice samples, and a POWEREDGEAR HIGHSCORE CAMPAIGN after the credits is absent. Devilotte's servants Dr. Shutain and Jigoku Daishi become Xavier and Gary, and Gawaine's sword Magnablade goes unnamed.

title: Darkstalkers: The Night Warriors
blurb: Capcom's 1994 CPS-II fighter unleashes vampires, werewolves and other night creatures on the arcade.
about: Released in July 1994 outside Japan, Darkstalkers: The Night Warriors is Capcom's North American and European version of the game known in Japan as Vampire: The Night Warriors. Several characters carry different names in these export versions: Gallon becomes Jon Talbain, Zabel Zarock becomes Lord Raptor, Aulbath becomes Rikuo, and Phobos becomes Huitzil. Justin Wong holds the official record with 687,800 points set on May 30, 2008, and a Darkstalkers unit appears in the 1995 movie The Net.

title: Dimahoo
blurb: Capcom's 2000 CPS-II shooter Dimahoo arrives in its North American and European arcade release.
about: A Capcom CPS-II arcade game from 2000, this is the North American and European release of Dimahoo, developed in Japan. It runs on the CP System II hardware, using the Blue Board configuration for USA and Europe.

title: Dungeons & Dragons: Shadow Over Mystara
blurb: Capcom's CPS-II sequel brings the Dungeons & Dragons arcade saga back for another round of monster-filled brawling.
about: A Capcom CPS-II arcade release from 1996, this is the North American and European version of Dungeons & Dragons: Shadow Over Mystara, developed in Japan. It runs on the CP System II hardware, specifically the Blue Board configuration used for USA and Europe.

title: Dungeons & Dragons: Tower of Doom
blurb: Capcom's 1994 CPS-II brawler brings the Dungeons & Dragons tabletop world to the arcade.
about: A Capcom CPS-II arcade title from 1994, this is the North American and European release of Dungeons & Dragons: Tower of Doom, with development handled in Japan. It runs on the CP System II hardware, on the Blue Board used for USA and Europe.

title: Eco Fighters
blurb: Capcom's 1993 CPS-II shooter sends you into battle to protect the planet's wildlife.
about: Eco Fighters is a Capcom arcade title released in 1993 on CP System II hardware. This North American and World release was developed in Japan, where it appeared under the title Ultimate Ecology. The game runs on the CP System II platform, specifically the Blue Board version distributed in the USA and other territories.

title: Giga Wing
blurb: A vertical shooter with frantic bullet patterns and massive scores arrives in North America.
about: Giga Wing is a Capcom arcade shooter released in North America on CPS-II hardware, developed in Japan. It runs on the Blue Board.

title: Hyper Street Fighter II: The Anniversary Edition
saveName: Hyper Street Fighter II: The Anniversary Edition
blurb: Capcom marks Street Fighter II's anniversary with a CPS-II fighter spanning every version.
about: Hyper Street Fighter II - The Anniversary Edition is Capcom's 2004 arcade fighter, released in North America on CPS-II hardware. The game was developed in Japan. For details about the game itself, see the original Japanese release entry, 'Hyper Street Fighter II - The Anniversary Edition [Green Board]'. This version runs on the blue board.
tips: Hyper Street Fighter II lets each player choose not only a fighter but also which version of that fighter to use: World Warrior, Champion Edition, Hyper Fighting, Super or Super Turbo.
Super Turbo versions of the fighters have Super Combos, while the older versions do not, so the mix-and-match makes for unusual match-ups.

title: Mars Matrix
blurb: Mars Matrix - Hyper Solid Shooting arrives as a 2000 Capcom CPS-II North American cart.
about: Mars Matrix - Hyper Solid Shooting is a 2000 Capcom Ent., Inc. CPS-II cart released in North America and developed in Japan. It runs on CP System II hardware on a Blue Board [USA], and is the North American counterpart to the Japanese release Mars Matrix - Hyper Solid Shooting [Green Board].

title: Marvel Super Heroes
blurb: Marvel Super Heroes lands on Capcom CPS-II in 1995 for North America and Europe.
about: Marvel Super Heroes is a 1995 Capcom Company, Limited CPS-II cart released in North America and Europe and developed in Japan. It runs on CP System II hardware on a Blue Board [USA & Europe], and is the regional counterpart to the Japanese release Marvel Super Heroes [Green Board]. It was released on October 24, 1995 (Tuesday).
tips: Infinity Gems drop during fights. Pick one up and activate it for a temporary power, such as more strength, speed or health recovery.
Thanos is the final boss, and many fighters can chain long air combos after launching an opponent.

title: Marvel Super Heroes vs. Street Fighter
saveName: Marvel Super Heroes vs. Street Fighter
blurb: Marvel Super Heroes vs. Street Fighter hits Capcom CPS-II in 1997 for the West.
about: Marvel Super Heroes vs. Street Fighter is a 1997 Capcom Company, Limited CPS-II cart released in North America and Europe and developed in Japan. It runs on CP System II hardware on a Blue Board [USA & Europe], and is the regional counterpart to the Japanese release Marvel Super Heroes vs. Street Fighter [Green Board].

title: Marvel vs. Capcom: Clash of Super Heroes
saveName: Marvel vs. Capcom: Clash of Super Heroes
blurb: Marvel heroes and Capcom fighters collide in a fast tag-team brawler built for the CPS-II arcade board.
about: Marvel vs. Capcom - Clash of Super Heroes is a 1998 Capcom arcade fighting game on CPS-II hardware, released in North America and Europe after its Japanese debut. When the announcer's lines were recorded, she had to say both the original Japanese character names and the export versions; alternate pronunciations were also taped, including a Chun-Li take where 'Chun' rhymes with 'fun' and an unused Zangief reading heard in the Sound Test.
tips: You pick two fighters and can tag between them during a match, plus a randomly chosen special partner who jumps in to assist a limited number of times per round.
The hyper combo gauge fills up to five levels. A Duo Team Attack fires both fighters' hyper combos at the same time.

title: Mega Man 2: The Power Fighters
blurb: Capcom's 1996 sequel brings more Robot Master duels to the CPS-II arcade board.
about: Mega Man 2 - The Power Fighters is Capcom's 1996 North American and European arcade release, developed in Japan and running on CP System II hardware. It continues the arcade fighting take on the Mega Man series.

title: Mighty! Pang
blurb: Mighty! Pang brings Mitchell Corp's 2000 bubble-bursting action to Capcom's CPS-II.
about: Mighty! Pang is a 2000 Mitchell Corp CPS-II cart released across North America and Europe and developed in Japan. It runs on CP System II hardware on a Blue Board [USA & Europe], and is the regional counterpart to the Japanese release Mighty! Pang [Green Board].

title: Night Warriors: Darkstalkers' Revenge
blurb: Capcom's Darkstalkers sequel brings its monster roster to Western arcades.
about: Night Warriors - Darkstalkers' Revenge is the North American and European release of Capcom's 1995 CPS-II fighting game, developed in Japan. For details on the game itself, see the original Japanese entry, Vampire Hunter - Darkstalkers' Revenge. The export versions dropped the expanded character epilogues found in the Japanese release, leaving only background character art. Several names were also changed for these versions: Gallon became Jon Talbain, Zabel Zarock became Lord Raptor, Aulbath became Rikuo, Phobos became Huitzil and Lei-Lei became Hsien-Ko.

title: Progear: Storm Of Progia
blurb: Capcom's bullet-hell shooter storms arcades with stylish steampunk dogfighting action.
about: Progear is a horizontally scrolling shoot-em-up released by Capcom in 2001 on CPS-II hardware. This entry is the North American release of the game developed in Japan. For details about the game itself, see the original Japanese release entry, Progear no Arashi.

title: Puzz Loop 2
blurb: Mitchell's 2001 puzzle sequel Puzz Loop 2 arrives on Capcom CPS-II hardware in its European release.
about: Puzz Loop 2 is a 2001 Mitchell Corp arcade game, released in Europe on a Capcom CPS-II cart and developed in Japan. It runs on CP System II hardware. For more on the game itself, see the original Japanese release entry, 'Puzz Loop 2 [Green Board]'.

title: Ring of Destruction: Slam Masters 2
blurb: Capcom's 1994 wrestling brawler Ring of Destruction: Slam Masters 2 hits the CPS-II ring.
about: Ring of Destruction: Slam Masters 2 is a 1994 Capcom arcade wrestling game running on CPS-II hardware, released in Europe and developed in Japan. It continues the Super Muscle Bomber series. Export versions renamed many fighters, though the Tokyo stage still shows their original Japanese names on a jumbo monitor before displaying the Super Muscle Bomber logo.

title: Street Fighter Alpha 2
blurb: Street Fighter Alpha 2, Capcom's 1996 CPS-II arcade sequel, arrived in North America and Europe.
about: Street Fighter Alpha 2 is a 1996 Capcom arcade fighting game on a CPS-II cartridge, released in North America and Europe and developed in Japan. For more about the game itself, see the original Japanese release entry, Street Fighter Zero 2 [Green Board]. Europe got it in February 1996 and the USA in March 1996. Export versions renamed Nash to Charlie, Vega to M. Bison, Gouki to Akuma, Shin Gouki to Shin Akuma, and Satsui no Hadou ni Mezameta Ryu to Evil Ryu. Japanese versions showed specific stage locations, while export versions listed only the country.

title: Street Fighter Alpha 3
blurb: Street Fighter Alpha 3, Capcom's 1998 CPS-II fighter, hit North American and European arcades.
about: Street Fighter Alpha 3 is a 1998 Capcom arcade fighting game on a CPS-II cartridge, released in North America and Europe and developed in Japan. For more about the game itself, see the original Japanese release entry, Street Fighter Zero 3 [Green Board]. Export versions renamed Gouki to Akuma, M. Bison to Balrog, Nash to Charlie, Vega to M. Bison, Shin Vega to Final Bison, and Balrog to Vega; in Europe and the Western Hemisphere the Z-ISM became A-ISM. Specific Japanese stage locations were dropped from export versions, leaving only country names.
tips: Before the fight you choose a style, called an ism: A-ism gives the usual three-level Super Combo gauge, X-ism plays like Super Turbo with a single powerful Super, and V-ism lets you start custom combos.

title: Street Fighter Alpha: Warriors' Dreams
blurb: Street Fighter Alpha: Warriors' Dreams brought Capcom's 1995 CPS-II fighter to North America and Europe.
about: Street Fighter Alpha - Warriors' Dreams is a 1995 Capcom USA arcade fighting game on a CPS-II cartridge, released in North America and Europe and developed in Japan. For more about the game itself, see the original Japanese release entry, Street Fighter Zero [Green Board]. This export version landed in June 1995. To stay consistent with earlier games, Nash became Charlie, Gouki became Akuma, and Vega became M. Bison. The Japanese version used an instrumental of 'Itoshisato Setsunasato Kokorotsuyosato' during Dramatic Battle mode, a change also made in the home ports.

title: Street Fighter Zero 2 Alpha
blurb: Capcom's 1996 arcade upgrade to Street Fighter Zero 2, packed with new moves and modes.
about: Street Fighter Zero 2 Alpha is an enhanced arcade edition of Street Fighter Zero 2, arriving in Japanese, Southeast Asian, Brazilian, and Hispanic arcades in August 1996. Outside those regions it reached players only on home consoles. It stays close to its predecessor while handing several fighters an extra move or two, and it adds modes including Dramatic Battle, Shin Akuma Mode, and Survival. The game runs on Capcom's CPS-II hardware.

title: Super Gem Fighter Mini Mix
blurb: Capcom's 1997 CPS-II fighter mixing Pocket Fighter action with gem-powered mini battles.
about: Super Gem Fighter - Mini Mix is the North American and European release of a Capcom fighting game built for CPS-II hardware and developed in Japan. It arrived in 1997. The Japanese arcade original is Pocket Fighter, released on a Green Board, while this version runs on a Blue Board. Details of the game itself are covered under that original entry.

title: Super Puzzle Fighter II Turbo
blurb: Capcom's 1996 puzzle spinoff brings Super Puzzle Fighter II Turbo to CPS-II arcade cabinets.
about: Super Puzzle Fighter II Turbo is a Capcom arcade title released in 1996 on the CP System II hardware, distributed as an export release with the game developed in Japan. This Blue Board version covers USA and Europe. It is the export counterpart to the original Japanese entry, Super Puzzle Fighter 2 II [Green Board].

title: Super Street Fighter II Turbo
blurb: Capcom's 1994 CPS-II fighter, where Akuma debuted overseas with his victory quotes and ending stripped out.
about: A 1994 Capcom arcade fighting game on CPS-II hardware, released outside Japan in February 1994 as the export version of Super Street Fighter II X - Grand Master Challenge. In these overseas releases, the character Gouki appears as Akuma, but all of his dialogue was removed rather than translated, leaving him without victory quotes and with no ending at all, only a credit roll and images of his defeated opponents.
tips: Super Turbo has seventeen fighters, adding Cammy, Fei Long, Dee Jay and T. Hawk from Super Street Fighter II, with Akuma as a hidden character.
It introduced the Super meter and Super Combos: fill the gauge, then perform a long special move input for a powerful finishing combo.

title: Vampire Hunter 2: Darkstalkers' Revenge
blurb: Fourteen hellish creatures clash for control of the nether-realms in Capcom's 1997 fighter.
about: Vampire Hunter 2: Darkstalkers' Revenge is a 1997 Capcom CPS-II arcade fighting game released only in Japan, where it was the 27th title for the CPS2 hardware. Up to two players battle with an 8-way joystick and six buttons covering light, medium, and heavy punches and kicks. Rather than a true sequel, it is a redesigned version built on the newest Darkstalkers engine, even reworking Vampire Savior 2's intro to remove references to Jedah, Bulleta, Q-Bee, and Lilith.

title: Vampire Savior 2
blurb: Fifteen fighters clash to stop Jedah in Capcom's 1997 CPS-II sequel, released in Japanese arcades.
about: Vampire Savior 2 - The Lord of Vampire is a 1997 Capcom fighting game on CPS-II hardware, where fifteen characters battle to end Jedah's reign and save their souls. It hit Japanese arcades in September 1997 as the 26th CPS2 title, supporting two players with an 8-way joystick and six buttons each. The intro hides a split-second montage of character sketches. Donovan's inclusion stems from a Capcom change: the original Vampire Savior draft had him turned into a demon and Anita added as a teen, but both were cut and only restored, ageless, here. The game isn't canon, partly due to Pyron, destroyed in the first tournament.

aka: Vampire Savior 2: The Lord of Vampire

title: Vampire Savior: The Lord Of Vampire
saveName: Vampire Savior: The Lord Of Vampire
blurb: Capcom's 1997 CPS-II fighter brings darkstalkers to battle, with renamed characters for Western arcades.
about: Vampire Savior - The Lord of Vampire is a 1997 Capcom arcade fighting game released on CPS-II hardware for North America and Europe. It was developed in Japan and runs on the CP System II, specifically the Blue Board for USA and Europe. In these export versions, several fighters carry different names: Bulleta becomes B. B. Hood, Lei-Lei is Hsien-Ko, Gallon is Jon Talbain, Zabel Zarock is Lord Raptor, and Aulbath is Rikuo.

title: X-Men vs Street Fighter
blurb: Capcom's 1996 CPS-II crossover X-Men vs. Street Fighter pits mutant against martial artist in arcades.
about: X-Men vs. Street Fighter is a 1996 Capcom Company, Limited arcade fighting game released for North America and Europe on CPS-II hardware, developed in Japan. It runs on the CP System II, specifically the Blue Board for USA and Europe.
tips: X-Men vs. Street Fighter was the first Capcom Vs. game with tag teams: pick two fighters and switch between them during the match.
The hyper combo gauge lets you chain long combos into Hyper Combos, and a Variable Attack brings your partner in with an attack.

title: X-Men: Children Of The Atom
blurb: Capcom's 1994 CPS-II fighter X-Men: Children of the Atom lands in North American and European arcades.
about: X-Men - Children of the Atom is a 1994 Capcom Company, Limited arcade fighting game released for North America and Europe on CPS-II hardware, developed in Japan. It runs on the CP System II, specifically the Blue Board for USA and Europe.

title: JoJo's Bizarre Adventure
blurb: Capcom's 1999 CPS-III fighter continues the JoJo saga with new characters and abilities.
about: Released by Capcom in 1999 for the CPS-III arcade system, this is the export version of the second JoJo fighting game. It continues the series' unique style of combat. For more information about the game itself, please see the original Japanese version entry, JoJo no Kimyou na Bouken - Mirai e no Isan.
tips: The Stand button summons or dismisses your Stand. With it out, your normal attacks and special moves change.
The game follows the third part of the JoJo's Bizarre Adventure manga, Stardust Crusaders, and its story mode covers the journey to fight Dio.

title: JoJo's Venture
blurb: Capcom's 1998 arcade fighter brings the bizarre world of JoJo to the CPS-III system.
about: This is the export version of Capcom's 1998 arcade fighting game, released for the CPS-III system. It is based on the popular manga and anime series JoJo's Bizarre Adventure. For details on the game itself, see the original Japanese version, JoJo no Kimyou na Bouken.

title: Red Earth
blurb: Capcom's 1996 CPS-III fantasy fighter Red Earth pits warriors against mighty beasts.
about: Red Earth is a Capcom arcade title released in October 1996 on the CPS-III hardware, known in Japan as War-Zard. It was the very first game produced for Capcom's Play System III board. This export release was developed in Japan and carries the distinction of launching a new generation of Capcom arcade hardware.

title: Street Fighter III: 2nd Impact
blurb: Street Fighter III: 2nd Impact - Giant Attack, Capcom's 1997 CPS-III sequel with Hugo and Urien.
about: Street Fighter III - 2nd Impact: Giant Attack is a 1997 Capcom arcade fighting game released as a CPS-III kit and the sequel to Street Fighter III - New Generation. It adds Hugo, Urien and returning character Akuma (Gouki in Japan), plus a speed increase, new moves and several damage-related tweaks. It launched on September 30, 1997. The 'Giant Attack' subtitle refers to the two huge new characters, Hugo and Urien. It is the only CPS3 game with a widescreen mode. Hugo is based on the late WWF Hall of Famer Andre The Giant, and Firstsmile released a limited-edition soundtrack album on December 17, 1997.

aka: Street Fighter III 2nd Impact: Giant Attack

title: Street Fighter III: 3rd Strike
blurb: Street Fighter III: 3rd Strike - Fight For The Future, Capcom's 1999 CPS-III arcade fighter.
about: Street Fighter III - 3rd Strike: Fight For The Future is a 1999 Capcom one-on-one fighting game for one or two players, released as a CPS-III kit and the second follow-up to Street Fighter III after 2nd Impact. It added five characters, including Chun-Li, plus Remy, Makoto, Q and Twelve, bringing the roster to twenty, and reintroduced the 'Destroy the Car' bonus stage. New mechanics include the Guard Parry, or 'Red Parry', letting players parry during guard stun with correct timing, and after-match evaluations grading Offense, Defence, Tech and Extra from E to MSF. It released in May 1999 and was the first Street Fighter game with a rap/hip hop urban theme.

aka: Street Fighter III 3rd Strike: Fight for the Future

tips: Parrying is the heart of the game: tap forward (or down, for low attacks) just as an attack lands to deflect it without taking damage.
Before each match you pick one of your fighter's three Super Arts, which decides the Super move you can use in that match.
Pressing two punch or two kick buttons for a special move does an EX version, which uses part of the Super meter.

title: Street Fighter III: New Generation
blurb: Street Fighter III: New Generation, Capcom's 1997 CPS-III arcade fighter with landmark 2-D animation.
about: Street Fighter III - New Generation is a 1997 Capcom arcade fighting game released as a CPS-III kit. It features larger character sprites than earlier Street Fighter games and, at release, the smoothest and most detailed 2-D animation ever made, a quality still unmatched outside the Street Fighter III series as of 2004; some critics felt too much was animated, slowing the pace. It hit Japanese arcades on February 17, 1997, and Capcom's flyer states animations run at up to 64 frames per second. The marquee simply calls it 'Three'. Sean was originally meant to be the only fighter using Ryu and Ken's style, with Ken and Ryu added later by fan demand.
tips: Before each match you choose one of three Super Arts for your fighter.
Tap forward just as an attack lands (or down for low attacks) to parry it and take no damage.

title: 3 Count Bout
blurb: SNK's 100-Mega Shock wrestling game pits 10 grapplers against each other in the ring.
about: Fire Suplex is a pro-wrestling game for the Neo-Geo MVS, known outside Japan as 3 Count Bout. Ten wrestlers bring Power Attacks and Malevolent Moves into the ring, biting, kicking, and punching toward the top spot, with competitive play and tag match battles. It supports two players with four buttons each. Released in Japan on March 25, 1993, it was developed by UPL and stands as the last game that manufacturer produced. It is the only 'true' wrestling title on the MVS hardware, with King of The Monsters predating it in the giant-monster sense. Game ID: NGM-043.

title: Aero Fighters 2
blurb: Eight pilots, eight jets, and randomized bosses fill Video System's 1994 Neo-Geo shooter Sonic Wings 2.
about: Sonic Wings 2 is a vertically scrolling shoot-em-up released by Video System on July 18, 1994, and known outside Japan as Aero Fighters 2. Players pick from eight fighter pilots, each flying a distinct jet such as the F-117A Nighthawk or the Rafale, battling jets, boats, helicopters, gun emplacements, and huge bosses whose identities change between playthroughs. Story and endings shift based on the pilot pair selected, with 47 endings in total, and the game famously blocks the initials 'SEX' on the high score table, changing them to 'OH!'. It runs on Neo-Geo MVS hardware under game ID NGM-075.
tips: Each pilot flies a different plane with its own shot and bomb, so the choice changes how the game plays.
Collect P items to power up your main shot. Bombs are limited and clear the bullets on screen, which makes them your escape button.

title: Aero Fighters 3
blurb: Video System's 1995 Neo-Geo shooter sends ten pilots worldwide to crush terrorism, then into outer space.
about: Sonic Wings 3 is the third entry in Video System's shoot-em-up series, released in October 1995 and known outside Japan as Aero Fighters 3. Players pilot jet fighters from country to country destroying terrorist forces before heading into outer space, with each pilot carrying a personal storyline. A single enemy shot destroys your plane and releases its power-up, and the space mission restarts from the beginning unless a second player is active. The game offers 23 endings, four random last bosses, and blocks the initials 'SEX', changing them to 'HEY'. It runs on Neo-Geo MVS hardware under game ID NGM-097.

title: Alpha Mission II
blurb: SNK's vertically scrolling Neo-Geo shooter, known outside Japan as Alpha Mission II.
about: ASO II - Last Guardian is SNK's full-screen vertically scrolling shoot'em up for the Neo-Geo MVS, released in Japan on March 25, 1991. Outside Japan it is known as Alpha Mission II. Game ID: NGM-007. Two players can join with four buttons each, three of them usable, and the controls differ by type: Type A maps missile/laser/attach armor, armor attack, and menu, while Type B maps laser/attach armor, missile, and menu.

title: Andro Dunos
blurb: Visco's 1992 Neo-Geo shooter lets you swap weapon types on the fly across a horizontal battlefield.
about: Andro Dunos is a horizontally scrolling shoot'em up released by Visco Corp in 1992 on SNK Neo-Geo MVS hardware. Players can switch between different weapon settings during play. Arriving on June 15, 1992, it holds the distinction of being Visco's first game developed and released for the SNK Neo-Geo MVS platform. Its Game ID is NGM-049.

title: Art of Fighting 2
blurb: SNK's 1994 Neo-Geo sequel pits 12 fighters against each other with visible damage accumulating in battle.
about: Ryuuko no Ken 2 is a martial arts fighting game released by SNK Corp in 1994 on Neo-Geo MVS hardware. It offers 12 selectable characters, each showing progressive damage on their bodies as the fight goes on. Released in Japan in March 1994 and known overseas as Art of Fighting 2, it includes a guest appearance by Geese Howard that ties its story to the Fatal Fury games. Its Game ID is NGM-056.

title: Art of Fighting 3
blurb: SNK's 1996 Neo-Geo fighter brings motion-captured animation and Mexican locales to the series.
about: Art of Fighting - Ryuuko no Ken Gaiden is a fighting game released by SNK Corp in 1996 on Neo-Geo MVS hardware. Ten selectable characters battle across various locations in Mexico, with fluid animation produced through motion capture technology. Released in Japan on March 12, 1996, its subtitle translates as 'Dragon and Tiger Fist Side Story' and it is known overseas as Art of Fighting 3. A limited-edition soundtrack album was issued by Pony Canyon / Scitron on 03/04/1996. Game ID: NGM-096.

aka: Art of Fighting 3: The Path of the Warrior
Art of Fighting: Ryuuko no Ken Gaiden

title: Bang Bead
blurb: Visco's 2001 Neo-Geo twist on Pong lets you pick a fighter and battle for the ball.
about: Bang Bead is a Neo-Geo MVS take on Pong, with a roster of selectable characters and a competitive two-player setup. Each player uses three of the four available buttons to return the ball, trigger a threat or slide, and unleash a Miracle Swing at maximum power. Arriving in May 2001 from Visco Corp, it ran on SNK's MVS hardware and appeared only in Europe. It never made it to the Neo-Geo AES home console.

title: Baseball Stars 2
blurb: SNK's 1992 sequel expands the diamond with 18 teams and deep league play.
about: Baseball Stars 2 is SNK's arcade baseball sequel, letting players build leagues of up to 125 games with six teams meeting 25 times. It tracks standings, average, home runs, RBIs, ERA, wins, and saves, and players can fire or upgrade athletes via the 15-point system from the original. Eighteen teams span the beginner Exciting League and expert Fighting League. Released in April 1992 for the Neo-Geo MVS, it supports two players with four buttons each.

title: Baseball Stars Professional
blurb: SNK's 1990 comical baseball game was the Neo-Geo MVS's first diamond outing.
about: Baseball Stars Professional is SNK's comical arcade baseball game, running on the Neo-Geo MVS with two players and four buttons each for batting, pitching, running, bunting, and timeouts. It hit arcades on April 26, 1990, and holds the distinction of being the first baseball game released for SNK's Neo-Geo MVS hardware.

title: Blazing Star
blurb: Yumekobo's 1998 Neo-Geo shooter follows six pilots turned against the machines.
about: Blazing Star is a horizontally scrolling shoot-'em-up set amid the endless war between Remuria and Mutras, where the sentient weapon Brawshella assimilates all life. Six assimilated pilots regain their humanity and fight back. Controlled with a joystick and two buttons, it offers normal, rapid, and charged shots plus a break attack. Released in January 1998, it was Yumekobo's first Neo-Geo MVS title, and a limited soundtrack album followed on March 18, 1998.

title: Blue's Journey
blurb: Alpha Denshi's 1991 Neo-Geo platformer sends Blue to save a polluted planet.
about: Raguy, known outside Japan as Blue's Journey, is an environmentally themed platformer for one or two players. The Daruma tribe is draining planet Raguy, so Blue (and Princess Fa in two-player mode) must clear fourteen stages across four worlds. Heroes stun foes with a large leaf, then throw them at other enemies, and can shrink to reach hidden areas. Released in March 1991 by Alpha Denshi Company, Limited, it runs on SNK's Neo-Geo MVS.

title: Breakers Revenge
blurb: Visco's 1998 Neo-Geo fighter adds Saizo and recolored stages to the Breakers lineup.
about: Breaker's Revenge is a modest update to Breakers, adding the new selectable fighter Saizo along with differently colored backgrounds. It runs on SNK's Neo-Geo MVS and supports two players with four buttons each for punches and kicks. Visco Corp released it in Japan on July 3, 1998, and it never appeared on the Neo-Geo AES home console. It was among the first four gigapower games, and a USA-bios coin-insert bug on single-slot cabinets was fixed afterward.

title: Burning Fight
blurb: Two NYPD detectives and a martial arts ally take on a Japanese crime syndicate in SNK's 1991 brawler.
about: Burning Fight is a 1991 SNK Neo-Geo MVS beat-'em-up in which New York detectives Duke and Billy pursue a dangerous Japanese crime syndicate. Their investigation brings them to Japan, where they team up with Ryu, a police officer and martial arts expert, to hunt down the syndicate bosses. Released in April 1991, the game runs on Neo-Geo MVS hardware with 2 players and 4 buttons each. Duke later appears as a striker in The King of Fighters 2000.

title: Crossed Swords
blurb: Become a wandering knight, slashing demons and casting spells in this 3rd-person fantasy action game.
about: A 3rd-person fantasy action game for the Neo-Geo, where you play a traveling knight helping those in need of a hero by cutting down the monsters and demons disrupting the peace. Your sword skills, spells and special weapons bought along the way carry you through the battle. Released in Japan on July 25, 1991, it was the Neo-Geo's second action-RPG after Riding Hero.

title: Crossed Swords 2
blurb: A pirate Neo-Geo take on the Crossed Swords CD adventure, released by Razoola.
about: Crossed Swords II is a pirate version of the CD game, released for SNK Neo-Geo MVS hardware by Razoola.

title: Double Dragon (Neo Geo)
blurb: Double Dragon's 1995 Neo Geo fighter turns the movie's martial arts showdown into a one-on-one tournament.
about: Based on the 1994 Double Dragon movie, this head-to-head fighter gathers series regulars Billy, Jimmy, Marian, Abobo and Burnov alongside five original characters, all competing in a martial arts tournament against crime lord Koga Shuko. Destructible environments and a super move meter that fills according to remaining energy give weaker fighters a fighting chance. Released in February 1995, it was Technos' first game for Neo-Geo hardware, and April Simmonds holds the official record with 96,700 points set on April 21, 2007.

title: EightMan
blurb: SNK's 1991 Neo-Geo brawler brings a classic anime hero to the arcade screen.
about: Eightman is a side-scrolling beat'em up and platform game released by SNK in 1991 for the Neo-Geo MVS. Developed by Pallas, it launched in September 1991 and draws from a Japanese cartoon series from the 1960s. The characters diverge from the traditional Eightman look, and Nineman is simply a palette swap of the main hero. Taiyo System later produced a pachislot adaptation in 2000.

title: Far East of Eden: Kabuki Klash
saveName: Far East of Eden: Kabuki Klash
blurb: Hudson's 1995 Neo-Geo fighter brings the Far East of Eden RPG world to the arcade.
about: This 1995 Neo-Geo MVS fighting game from Hudson Soft features eight selectable characters and four end-bosses, with random bonus items appearing during battles. It is a Japanese swordplay fighter set in the Far East of Eden RPG universe. Released in Japan in June 1995, it was Hudson's first game for the Neo-Geo MVS. A limited-edition soundtrack was released by Pony Canyon / Scitron on 17/11/1995.

title: Fatal Fury
blurb: SNK's 1991 fighter launches Terry Bogard on a quest for revenge in the King of Fighters.
about: Fatal Fury is a 1991 SNK Neo-Geo MVS fighting game known in Japan as Garou Densetsu - Shukumei no Tatakai. Terry and Andy Bogard enter the King of Fighters tournament to find their father's killer, the sponsor and champion Geese Howard. Two-plane backgrounds give battles a pseudo 3-D feel. Originally titled Real Bout, the game introduced Terry Bogard, who became one of SNK's most recognizable fighters.

title: Fatal Fury 3: Road to the Final Victory
saveName: Fatal Fury 3: Road to the Final Victory
blurb: SNK's 1995 fighter follows the lone wolves into a battle over the Shiranui Scrolls.
about: Fatal Fury 3: Road to the Final Victory is an SNK Neo-Geo MVS fighting game released in 1995, known in Japan as Garou Densetsu 3 - Harukanaru Tatakai. Terry, Andy, Joe, and Mai get caught in a hunt for the Shiranui Scrolls. The game introduced a deeper plane-change system, chain combos, and new fighters including Blue Mary and Ryuji Yamazaki. A limited soundtrack album came from Pony Canyon on April 21, 1995.

title: Fatal Fury Special
blurb: SNK's 1993 special edition of Fatal Fury 2 packs new fighters and refined combat.
about: Fatal Fury Special is an SNK Neo-Geo MVS fighting game from 1993, known in Japan as Garou Densetsu Special. It builds on Fatal Fury 2 with two-plane backgrounds, tighter controls, and plenty of secrets. Duck King, Tung Fu Rue, Geese Howard, and Ryo Sakazaki join the roster. The combo system was refined, damage reduced, and game speed increased. A limited soundtrack album arrived via Pony Canyon on 21/10/1993.

title: Ganryu
blurb: A Neo-Geo sword-fighting tale inspired by the legendary duel of Musashi and Kojiro.
about: Musashi Ganryuki is a fighting game released by Visco in 1999 for the SNK Neo-Geo MVS. Known outside Japan as Ganryu, its title translates as 'Musashi Ganryu Tale'. Two players choose fighters and use an 8-way joystick with buttons for sword attack, jump, and chain attack. The game draws on the famous 1612 duel in which Musashi defeated Sasaki Ganryu Kojiro with a wooden sword carved from a boat oar. Kojiro appears with a huge gash on his forehead, and the storyline has him returning from the dead to kill Musashi. The game runs on Neo-Geo MVS but was never released on the Neo-Geo AES home console.

title: Ghost Pilots
blurb: Two ace pilots take on Axis forces in SNK's 1991 vertical World War II shoot-em-up.
about: Ghost Pilots is SNK's 1991 vertically-scrolling shoot-em-up for one or two players, set in World War II. Freelance aces Tom Phillips and Charlie Stingley, the 'Ghost Pilots', fly seaplanes against an ambitious Nazi general's forces. Before each stage you pick one of two bomb types, and in certain later stages a third unique bomb becomes available. You start with three bombs and can carry up to nine. Shooting a row of red planes drops power-ups, bombs, or extra lives.

title: Goal! Goal! Goal!
blurb: Pick from 28 national teams and battle through group and knockout rounds in this Neo-Geo soccer classic.
about: Goal! Goal! Goal! is a 1995 Neo-Geo MVS soccer game from Visco Corp that pits 28 national teams against each other in a tournament. Play starts with a group stage, then moves into a round-robin elimination phase where one loss can end your run. Hold the shoot button to fill the power bar and unleash a powerful super shot. The game ran on SNK's Neo-Geo MVS hardware and never saw a Neo-Geo AES home console release.

title: Karnov's Revenge
blurb: Data East's 1994 fighter returns with faster combat and new moves on Neo-Geo MVS.
about: This 1994 Neo-Geo MVS fighter is the sequel to Fighter's History. It features faster, more technical battles, new hidden moves, and an enhanced color palette. The game is known as Karnov's Revenge in Europe and Fighter's History Dynamite in Japan and the USA. Released on March 17, 1994, it was the third Data East game made for Neo-Geo hardware. It switched from a six-button to a four-button control scheme and added new stages, music, and endings for every character.

title: Last Resort
blurb: SNK's 1992 Neo-Geo shooter drops you into a city that echoes Neo Tokyo from Akira.
about: Last Resort is an SNK Neo-Geo MVS release from 1992. Two players can team up, each using two of the four available buttons for attacking and charging attacks. The opening two stages feature a city strongly resembling Neo Tokyo from the anime film Akira. A limited-edition soundtrack album was issued by Pony Canyon / Scitron on 21/05/1992.

title: League Bowling (Neo Geo)
blurb: SNK's 1990 Neo-Geo ten-pin game bowls up three scoring modes for one to four players.
about: SNK's 1990 Neo-Geo MVS release is a colourful ten-pin bowling game for one to four players with three scoring methods: Regulation, Flash and Strike 90. You choose a right- or left-handed bowler and ball weight, then time Power and Direction meters within twenty seconds per shot. Strike 90 awards ninety points for a strike and sixty for a spare, while Flash adds the points shown when pins fall. Released on December 10, 1990, it includes a cameo by Nadia from Secret of Blue Water in the background.

title: Magical Drop II
blurb: Data East's 1996 Neo-Geo puzzler proves that puzzle games can be furiously fast-paced.
about: Magical Drop II arrived on SNK's Neo-Geo MVS in 1996 from Data East. Two players grab an 8-way joystick and two buttons to catch and throw balloons in hectic puzzle battles with lively animations and music. The roster draws loosely on figures from well-known Tarot cards, and a limited-edition soundtrack album came out via Pony Canyon / Scitron on June 21, 1996.

title: Magical Drop III Toretate Zoukangou!
blurb: Data East's final arcade game brings more characters and more frantic balloon-matching chaos.
about: Magical Drop III hit the Neo-Geo MVS in 1997 from Data East, expanding the puzzle action with extra characters and modes for one or two players. A joystick and three buttons let you catch, throw, and shift balloons downward. It stands as Data East's last arcade video game, and its cast parodies all 22 Major Arcana Tarot cards, numbered 0 through 21, plus the bonus character Black Pierrot. A limited-edition soundtrack landed March 21, 1997.

title: Magician Lord
blurb: Alpha Denshi's 1990 Neo-Geo debut casts you as Elta, the last Magician Lord.
about: Magician Lord launched on SNK's Neo-Geo MVS in 1990 from Alpha Denshi. You guide the wizard Elta through eight side-scrolling stages, jumping and firing energy shots in four directions while collecting colored orbs to transform into six different powerful forms. It was Alpha Denshi's first Neo-Geo title and the first game to exploit the hardware's dezooming and rotation. Though 27 transformations were planned, only six made the final cut.

title: Matrimelee
blurb: The Goketsuji clan returns on Neo-Geo with fresh fighters and a wild marriage battle.
about: Matrimelee came to SNK's Neo-Geo MVS from Playmore in 2002, reviving the Gouketsuji / Power Instinct series. Two players use an 8-way joystick and four buttons for weak and strong punches and kicks, with 11 familiar faces joined by four newcomers. Developed by Noise Factory and Atlus, it officially reached the public in March 2003 despite its 2002 copyright. Its Japanese soundtrack is notable for an unusually large number of vocal tracks across many stages.

title: Metal Slug
blurb: Metal Slug's 1996 Neo-Geo debut delivers run-and-gun war parody for one or two players.
about: Metal Slug - Super Vehicle-001 is Nazca's 1996 SNK Neo-Geo MVS scrolling run-and-gun platform game for one or two players, a humorous parody of war and specifically World War II and the Nazis. It spans six enemy-packed levels called missions, starting players with only a pistol while extra weapons can be picked up for greater firepower. At certain points players find an unused Super Vehicle-001, or Metal Slug, tank to enter and drive; it is slow but heavily armed, and if it takes too many hits it breaks down and flashes, forcing a quick exit before it explodes. Enemies field tanks, boats, and helicopters, and levels are littered with bearded hostages who award points bonuses or weapon…
tips: Rescue the tied-up prisoners of war for bonus points at the end of each mission; many of them hand you a weapon or an item.
The weapon crates carry a letter: H is the Heavy Machine Gun, R the Rocket Launcher, F the Flame Shot and S the Shotgun. Each has limited ammo, and you fall back to the pistol when it runs out.
Grenades are limited (you start with ten), so save them for armored targets and bosses. Attack an enemy at close range and you use a knife instead of a bullet.
Climb into the SV-001 tank, the Metal Slug itself, when you find it: it fires its cannon with the grenade button and takes a few hits before it is destroyed.

title: Metal Slug 3
blurb: SNK's 2000 Neo-Geo classic sends Marco and Tarma against Morden's army, with branching routes and wild transformations.
about: Metal Slug 3 is a side-scrolling run-and-gun action game released by SNK in 2000 for the Neo-Geo MVS. Players control returning heroes from the first two games as they battle General Morden's forces, with a heavier focus on massive boss encounters than its predecessors. Most levels offer multiple paths, such as choosing between land or a submarine on the first stage, boosting replay value. Picking up too much food turns characters obese, while zombie attacks cause zombification, and the Mars People aliens in Mission 5 reference Independence Day.
tips: Several missions split into different routes, so two runs through the same mission can look quite different.
Metal Slug 3 has the biggest vehicle line-up of the early games, including the Slug Mariner submarine, the Elephant Slug, the Ostrich Slug, the Drill Slug and the Slugnoid walker.
Get hit by a zombie's attack and you turn into one: slow, but with a powerful vomit attack, until a medical item turns you back.
There are five missions, and the last one is famously long, ending in space.

title: Metal Slug 4
blurb: Playmore's 2002 Neo-Geo entry pits four heroes against the Amadeus cyber-terror threat and a still-living Morden.
about: Metal Slug 4 is a side-scrolling action game released by Playmore Corp in 2002 for the Neo-Geo MVS. A computer virus from the terrorist group Amadeus threatens every nation's military systems, and four heroes—Marco Rossi, Fio Germi, Nadia Cassel and Trevor Spacey—set out to stop it, discovering along the way that Morden is still alive. The game was developed by South Korean company Mega Enterprise, which had held SNK copyrights for South Korea since 1999. A hack version is known as Metal Slug 4 Plus.

title: Metal Slug 5
blurb: SNK Playmore's 2003 Neo-Geo chapter sends Marco, Tarma, Eri and Fio after the Ptolemaic Army and stolen Metal Slug secrets.
about: Metal Slug 5 is a side-scrolling action game released by SNK Playmore in 2003 for the Neo-Geo MVS. After unknown forces raid a research site and steal a disk of Metal Slug secrets, Marco and Tarma give chase while Eri and Fio investigate the Ptolemaic Army at the ancient ruin called The Corridor of Fire. This entry added a slide move performed by holding the B button, and players can fire while sliding. A hack version is known as Metal Slug 5 Plus.
tips: Metal Slug 5 adds a slide move to the series, letting you dash under bullets and enemies.
The enemy this time is the Ptolemaic Army rather than General Morden's rebels.

title: Metal Slug X
blurb: SNK's 1999 Neo-Geo remaster of Metal Slug 2 fixes slowdown and adds new enemies, weapons, secrets and a reworked final boss.
about: Metal Slug X - Super Vehicle-001 is a side-scrolling run-and-gun game released by SNK in 1999 for the Neo-Geo MVS. It was built to address problems in Metal Slug 2, most notably the notorious slowdown, while also adding new enemies, a different end boss layout and extra weapons and secrets. During the credits, up to five different sets of twelve character, enemy and vehicle artwork images can appear.
tips: Metal Slug X is a reworked Metal Slug 2 with new routes, new weapons and far less slowdown.
Eat too much food and your soldier gets fat: slower, but with stronger shots. Mummy gas turns you into a mummy until you find an antidote.
New weapons include the Iron Lizard, the Enemy Chaser, the Drop Shot and the Super Grenade, on top of the series' Heavy Machine Gun, Rocket Launcher, Flame Shot, Shotgun and Laser.
Four soldiers can be picked: Marco, Tarma, Eri and Fio.

title: Mutation Nation
blurb: SNK's 1992 Neo-Geo brawler sends two mutant-powered warriors into a futuristic wasteland to restore order.
about: Mutation Nation is a side-scrolling beat-'em-up released by SNK in March 1992 for the Neo-Geo MVS. Two lone warriors wielding special mutant powers fight to bring order back to a futuristic wasteland. Each player uses a four-button layout, with attack and jump as the two functional inputs.

title: NAM-1975
blurb: Two soldiers blast into the Vietnam war's final months to rescue a kidnapped scientist and his daughter.
about: NAM-1975 is SNK's 1990 Neo-Geo MVS war-themed shoot-em-up for one or two players, following soldiers Silver and Brown as they enter the conflict to rescue Dr. R. Muckly and his daughter Nancy from the Northside Terrorists. Played from a third-person into-the-screen view, it arms players with an infinite-ammo machine gun and ten grenades, with stronger guns and grenades dropped by certain enemies. Released April 26, 1990 in Japan, it was the first game developed for the Neo-Geo MVS hardware and drew influence from Stanley Kubrick's 1987 film Full Metal Jacket.

title: Neo Bomberman
blurb: Hudson's bomb-dropping multiplayer favorite lands on the Neo-Geo MVS with one-button mayhem.
about: Neo Bomber Man is a 1997 Hudson Soft arcade game released on SNK's Neo-Geo MVS hardware, with a single button handling bomb setting, kicking and throwing for two players. It came out in May 1997 in Japan and, despite running on the MVS, never saw a release on the Neo-Geo AES home console.
tips: Drop bombs to break the soft blocks and catch your rivals in the blast; a bomb's flames run along rows and columns.
Power-ups hide under the soft blocks: the fire item lengthens your blast, the bomb item lets you place more bombs at once and the skate makes you faster.

title: Neo Drift Out
blurb: Pick your rally car and race six stages against the clock in this isometric Neo-Geo racer.
about: Neo Drift Out - New Technology is an overhead isometric rally racer from Visco, released on SNK's Neo-Geo MVS in 1996. You choose between the Mitsubishi Lancer, Subaru Impreza or Toyota Celica, each with its own balance of Speed, Control and Body. After a short practice stage, up to six race stages await, each with unique locations and driving conditions. You must reach the finish before the timer runs out, hitting a mid-way checkpoint along the way. Arrows warn of corners, prompts flag hazards like ice, rocks, barrels, cones and ramps, and rival drivers can ram you into a spin. It hit Japanese arcades on March 28, 1996.

title: Neo Mr. Do!
blurb: Visco's Neo-Geo take on the classic Mr. Do! formula, made for two players.
about: Neo Mr. Do! is a Visco Corp arcade title released on SNK's Neo-Geo MVS hardware in 1996. It supports two players, using an 8-way joystick with a single attack button. Despite arriving on the MVS platform, the game never saw a release on the Neo-Geo AES home console.

title: Neo Turf Masters
blurb: Choose from six golfers with distinct strengths and tee off across four eighteen-hole courses.
about: Big Tournament Golf is an arcade golf game from Nazca Corporation, released in January 1996 for the Neo-Geo MVS. One or two players pick from six golfers, each with different driving, accuracy, skill, recovery, and putting ratings. Four eighteen-hole courses are available: Germany, Japan, Australia, and U.S.A. Modes include one-player stroke play against the CPU, or stroke and match-play against a second player. Known outside Japan as Neo Turf Masters, it was Nazca's first game for the Neo-Geo MVS.

title: Nightmare in the Dark
blurb: A gravekeeper battles zombies and night dwellers in this charming Neo-Geo action game.
about: Nightmare in the Dark is a 2000 Neo-Geo MVS release from Eleven and Gavaking. A peaceful but creepy-looking gravekeeper takes the night shift to stop a grave-robbing mystery before the villagers panic. The action follows the Snow Bros., Tumble Pop and Zupapa! style, backed by detailed graphics and a strong soundtrack. Two players can join in with an 8-way joystick and three buttons. It launched in January 2000, never appeared on the Neo-Geo AES, and famously swaps the initials 'SEX' to 'KING' on its high score table.

title: Ninja Combat
blurb: Storm the ninja castle and turn defeated bosses into playable fighters.
about: Ninja Combat is a 1990 Neo-Geo MVS arcade game from Alpha Denshi Company, Limited, in which players invade a ninja castle. Beating certain boss enemies makes them playable characters as well. It launched in July 1990.

title: Ninja Commando
blurb: Three ninjas chase a madman named Spider through time to stop him rewriting history.
about: Ninja Commando is a 1992 Neo-Geo MVS arcade title from Alpha Denshi Company, Limited, sending three ninjas after a madman named Spider who aims to use a time machine to tamper with history. It plays as a tongue-in-cheek reworking of Time Soldiers, which Alpha Denshi made five years earlier, this time with ninjas as the heroes. It was released on April 30, 1992.

title: Over Top
blurb: Race varied vehicles through handsome backdrops and hunt down hidden shortcuts.
about: Over Top is a 1996 Neo-Geo MVS racer from ADK that presents 3D-like action with 2D visuals and notably well-crafted backgrounds. You drive a range of different vehicles. The goal is to finish every race before the clock runs out, and the stages hide plenty of shortcuts to discover. It arrived in April 1996, supports two players, and uses an 8-way joystick with two buttons: one to accelerate and one to slow down.

title: Panic Bomber
blurb: Bomber formations collide in this Neo-Geo puzzler from Eighting and Hudson Soft.
about: Panic Bomber brings formation-based puzzle action to the Neo-Geo MVS. You rearrange falling bombers with the joystick and a single button to clear the board and outlast your opponent. Hudson Soft developed the game, which first appeared on the PC-Engine CD as Panic Bomber - Bomber Man. The arcade version hit Neo-Geo MVS in January 1995 but never made it to the AES home console.

title: Prehistoric Isle 2
blurb: Two high-tech helicopters battle a dinosaur invasion in this Neo-Geo shooter sequel.
about: Prehistoric Isle 2 is a side-scrolling shooter set in a future overrun by dinosaurs. You pilot one of two helicopters: the Blue One fires a wide straight shot with a wave-cannon bomb, while the Green One uses a spread shot and grenade barrage. Rescuing civilian survivors earns points and power-ups. Released in September 1999 by Yumekobo, it runs on Neo-Geo MVS but never saw an AES home release. In Japan it is known as Prehistoric Isle 2 - Genshi Tou.

title: Pulstar
blurb: A lone pilot faces an alien invasion in this visually stunning Neo-Geo shoot-em-up.
about: Pulstar is a side-scrolling shooter set in 2248, after a signal from Mars draws an alien fleet that devastates the Solar System. You fly the Dino246 as Kaoru Yamazaki, one of the last survivors of the Pulstar attack force. The game borrows heavily from Irem's R-Type series, including the Beam weapon and pod attachment. Released in August 1995 by Aicom, it was among the first Neo-Geo titles to use SGI-rendered graphics. Its pre-production name was Reaction.

title: Puzzle Bobble
blurb: Taito's bubble-popping puzzler lands on Neo-Geo MVS with two-player color-matching action.
about: Puzzle Bobble comes to the Neo-Geo MVS as a conversion of Taito's B System original. Aim and fire bubbles to match three or more of the same color and clear the playfield. This MVS release arrived in December 1994 and was Taito's first game on the hardware, six months after the B System original. A limited-edition soundtrack, Puzzle Bobble Variety, was released by Zuntata Records on March 28, 1997.
tips: Aim the launcher at the bottom of the screen and fire bubbles; three or more of the same colour touching each other pop.
Bounce shots off the side walls to reach awkward spots. The ceiling drops lower over time, and bubbles reaching the bottom line end the round.

title: Puzzle Bobble 2 / Bust-A-Move 2
blurb: SNK's MVS conversion of the bubble-bursting classic, known in the US as Bust-A-Move Again.
about: Puzzle Bobble 2 arrives on Neo-Geo MVS as a conversion of Taito's original F3 title. Fire bubbles, match colors, and clear the board before your rival does. In North America the game is called Bust-A-Move Again, and its marquee and fliers even billed it as Bust-A-Move Again EX. While the original US F3 release swapped out Bub and Bob for generic hands, this MVS port keeps the original Puzzle Bobble 2 assets. It is also noted as the first coin-op to coin-op port.

title: Rage of the Dragons
blurb: Rage of the Dragons brings 14 fighters plus hidden boss Abubo to the Neo-Geo in 2002.
about: Rage of the Dragons is a 2002 Playmore Corp fighting game on Neo-Geo MVS, offering 14 selectable fighters along with Abubo as sub-boss and Johann as the final boss. Four buttons cover weak and strong punches and kicks. Released in June 2002, it was Evoga Entertainment's first fighting game, made with Brezza Soft and Noise Factory after Technos Japan declined to sell the Double Dragon rights, so the team built an homage instead.

title: Real Bout Fatal Fury
blurb: SNK's 1995 fighter Real Bout Fatal Fury brings 16 fighters and plane-switching to the Neo-Geo.
about: Real Bout Garou Densetsu is a 1995 SNK Neo-Geo MVS fighting game, known outside Japan as Real Bout Fatal Fury. Its 16-character roster mixes old and new faces to refresh the Fatal Fury series, using a four-button setup (punch, kick, power attack, plane switch). Released in Japan on December 21, 1995, it stands out as one of the few 2-D fighters with ring outs. Newcomers include Kim Kaphwan, Duck King and Billy Kane, and Pony Canyon put out a limited-edition soundtrack on 07/02/1996.

title: Real Bout Fatal Fury 2: The Newcomers
saveName: Real Bout Fatal Fury 2: The Newcomers
blurb: Real Bout Fatal Fury 2: The Newcomers packs 23 South Town fighters into SNK's 1998 Neo-Geo bout.
about: Real Bout Garou Densetsu 2 - The Newcomers is a 1998 SNK Corp Neo-Geo MVS fighter, the 7th installment in the series, known outside Japan as Real Bout Fatal Fury 2 - The Newcomers. It brings 23 South Town fighters and returns to single-plane stages where you can slam enemies into background objects. Shown at the 1998 AOU Amusement Expo in Japan and released that March, it adds Li Xiangfei, Rick Strowd and Alfred. It's one of the first four 'gigapower' games, and Pony Canyon / Scitron released a limited-edition soundtrack on April 17, 1998.

aka: Real Bout Garou Densetsu 2: The Newcomers

title: Real Bout Fatal Fury Special
blurb: SNK's 1997 Real Bout Fatal Fury Special brings 19 selectable fighters to the Neo-Geo MVS.
about: Real Bout Garou Densetsu Special is a 1997 SNK Corp Neo-Geo MVS fighter, known outside Japan as Real Bout Fatal Fury Special. It returns more Fatal Fury favorites, raising the selectable roster to 19, and tweaks the plane-switching system while turning ring outs into an instant dizzy system triggered by breaking background objects. Though the copyright reads 1996, it launched in Japan on January 28, 1997. Newcomers include Cheng Sinzan, Tung Fu Rue, Laurence Blood and Wolfgang Krauser, with 'evil' character versions also available.

title: Robo Army
blurb: SNK's 1991 Robo Army sends two cyber soldiers against the invading Hell Jeed army.
about: Robo Army is a 1991 SNK Neo-Geo MVS side-scrolling beat-em-up for one or two players, starring cyber soldiers Rocky and Maxima battling the Hell Jeed army. Three buttons handle attack, jump, and energy blast. Released in Japan on October 30, 1991, the game lets players rip weakened enemies in half and even club robots with fallen limbs. Rocky later appeared as a striker in The King of Fighters 2000.

title: Samurai Shodown III
blurb: Twelve fighters take on the demon samurai Zankuro in SNK's 1995 weapons-based fighter.
about: Samurai Spirits - Zankurou Musouken is a weapons-based fighting game from SNK, released in October 1995 on the Neo-Geo MVS. Twelve selectable characters fight to defeat Zankuro, a very powerful demon samurai. Known outside Japan as Samurai Shodown III and in Korea as Fighters Swords, its full US name is Samurai Shodown III - Blades of Blood. The subtitle translates as 'Zankuro's Matchless Sword'. Kafuin Gaira, a Buddhist monk, wields giant mala prayer beads.

title: Samurai Shodown IV: Amakusa's Revenge
blurb: Seventeen fighters and two bosses clash in SNK's 1996 weapons-based fighter with CD combos and fatalities.
about: Samurai Shodown IV: Amakusa's Revenge is the fourth entry in SNK's weapons-based one-on-one fighting series, released on October 25, 1996 on the Neo-Geo MVS. It features seventeen selectable characters and two end bosses. The formula changed with the removal of aerial blocking, the switch-around move, dodges, and POW gauge charging. A new CD combo was added, along with a suicide move that forfeits a round but grants a full POW gauge next round, plus certain fatalities. Older characters like Charlotte, Tam Tam, and Jubei Yagyu returned.

title: Samurai Shodown V Special
blurb: SNK Playmore's 2004 Samurai Shodown V Special adds four fighters to the Neo-Geo roster.
about: Samurai Shodown V Special is a 2004 SNK Playmore Neo-Geo MVS fighter, upgrading Samurai Spirits Zero with its 24 fighters plus Amakusa, Gaoh, Zankuro, and Mizuki. Four buttons handle light and medium attacks, kick/break defence, and dodges. Released in Japan in April 2004, it is often called the ultimate MVS title, arriving as SNK Playmore shifted development to AtomisWave. Corrected cartridges added missing fatalities, marked by a small NeoGeo sticker.

title: Sengoku
blurb: Two spiritually gifted warriors battle to stop the Mad Shogun's resurrection in this 1991 Neo-Geo brawler.
about: Sengoku Densyo is a 1991 Neo-Geo MVS game from SNK, released on February 12, 1991 in Japan and known outside Japan as Sengoku. Two warriors with spiritual gifts fight to stop the resurrection of the Mad Shogun, facing strange enemies and striking scenery, with the ability to morph into different fighters. Items change special attacks: ten green items grant a 1-up, while red, blue, and purple grant a samurai sword, double sword, and holy sword. A level 2 background store, 'Boutique Athena', shows the original 1986 Athena logo.

title: Sengoku 2
blurb: The Mad Shogun returns to conquer the timestream in this 1993 Neo-Geo sequel with permanent sword combat.
about: Sengoku Densyo 2 is a 1993 Neo-Geo MVS game from SNK, released on February 18, 1993 in Japan and known outside Japan as Sengoku 2. The Mad Shogun rises again, taking over various periods in the time stream. Players are permanently armed with a sword and must save different eras from the Mad Shogun's wrath. On foot, buttons handle slicing, severing, jumping, and changing form; on a horse, they handle forward and rear attacks.

title: Sengoku 3
blurb: SNK's 2001 Neo-Geo brawler brings fighting-game depth with chain combos and stashable throwing weapons.
about: Sengoku 3 is a horizontally-scrolling beat-em-up for one or two players, released in October 2001 on the Neo-Geo MVS. It stands out for its complex chain-combo combat system, using light, heavy, and long-ranged attack buttons rather than simple mashing. Each of the four playable characters has directional special moves and a super bar with several super moves. Players can stash one type of ranged weapon, including shuriken, bombs, and kunai, and weave them into combos. It was developed by Noise Factory as their first game and was SNK's last official title.

title: Shock Troopers
blurb: SNK's 1997 Neo Geo shooter sends one or two troopers through three branching mission routes.
about: Shock Troopers is SNK's 1997 multi-directional scrolling shooter for one or two players, built on the foundations of Capcom's Commando and Mercs. Players fight a terrorist group holding a girl hostage to force her grandfather into surrendering a mind-controlling drug. Alongside enemy troops come tanks, choppers, and landmines, with weapons and health found in destroyed vehicles and supply crates. Three selectable routes make it effectively three games in one, and stages include vehicle chases and rock climbing. It released in November 1997 and never came to the Neo-Geo AES home console.

title: Shock Troopers - 2nd Squad
blurb: SNK's 1998 Neo Geo run-and-gun returns with sharper graphics and more inventive level design.
about: Shock Troopers - 2nd Squad is SNK's 1998 Neo Geo follow-up to the previous year's game. One or two players battle a terrorist army threatening to unleash a new weapon of mass destruction unless it is handed control of the new nation of Billberk. More an update than a full sequel, it polishes the graphics and offers more imaginative level design than the original. It arrived in October 1998, and Pony Canyon / Scitron issued a limited-edition soundtrack in January 1999.

title: SNK vs. Capcom: SVC Chaos
blurb: The 2003 Neo-Geo crossover fighter pitting seventeen SNK combatants against seventeen Capcom characters.
about: A one-on-one fighting game released in July 2003 by Playmore on SNK Neo-Geo MVS hardware, SVC Chaos - SNK Vs. Capcom pits seventeen well-known SNK combatants against seventeen famous Capcom characters. It mainly uses the command system of the King of Fighters series, with light and strong kicks and punches, cancels and charging attacks, and unlike Capcom vs. SNK 2 it has no air guards and no groove system, focusing instead on quicker play and online competition. Each character has a basic three-bar system for executing Exceeds, filled by strikes and damage, and the sprites from the various series received new models while some command-list special effects changed.

title: Soccer Brawl
blurb: SNK's futuristic soccer arcade game from 1992 mixes power shots, sliding cuts, and arm punches on the Neo-Geo.
about: Soccer Brawl is a futuristic soccer game released by SNK in February 1992 for the Neo-Geo MVS arcade hardware. Two players face off using four buttons each, with two in use: attack with a kick or power shot, and pass, while defence offers a sliding cut or arm punch and a header. It runs on SNK's Neo-Geo MVS platform under game ID NGM-031.

title: Spinmaster
blurb: Johnny and Tom chase map pieces and rescue Mary in Data East's 1993 Neo-Geo platformer, known as Spinmaster.
about: Miracle Adventure, known outside Japan as Spinmaster, is a platformer released by Data East on December 16, 1993, and the company's first game developed for the SNK Neo-Geo MVS hardware. Two treasure seekers, Johnny and Tom, must save their friend Mary from the evil Mad Doctor and his henchmen while gathering map pieces to find the world's biggest treasure. The game features cartoon-like character designs, giant bosses such as a Chinese dragon, and fast platforming, with a style heavily inspired by Data East's Caveman Ninja. It runs under game ID NGM-062 with three buttons: shoot or power attack, jump, and super attack.

title: Street Hoop
blurb: Data East's 1994 Neo-Geo street basketball game: pick one of ten countries for three-on-three slamdunkin' action.
about: A Data East basketball game on SNK Neo-Geo MVS hardware, released in Japan on December 8, 1994 as Dunk Dream and known outside Japan as Street Hoop and in the US as Street Slam. Ten countries are selectable for three-on-three street action. Two players share an 8-way joystick and two buttons: on offense A shoots or dunks and B passes, while on defense A blocks a shot and B steals the ball. A limited-edition soundtrack, Dunk Dream / Gun Hard, was released by Pony Canyon / Scitron on January 20, 1995.

title: Super Dodge Ball
blurb: Three-on-three dodge ball with special moves and team attacks hits the Neo-Geo MVS in 1996.
about: Super Dodge Ball is a 1996 Neo-Geo MVS game from Technos Japan Corp, known in Japan as Kunio no Nekketsu Toukyuu Densetsu. Teams of three try to knock each other out using special moves and team attacks. You control a team and must beat all others, even recruiting defeated leaders, to face the reigning champion. It features anime-style graphics and runs on Neo-Geo MVS but was never released on the Neo-Geo AES home console. Technos Japan went bankrupt on December 15, 1995.

title: The Irritating Maze
blurb: Guide a stick through a maze without touching the walls in this SNK trackball challenge from 1997.
about: Based on a Japanese game show, this SNK title for the Neo-Geo MVS challenges players to navigate a stick through a maze without touching the sides. It is a test of steady nerves and precision. Released in Japan in August 1997, it was the first Neo-Geo MVS game to require a trackball and was never ported to the home Neo-Geo AES console.

title: The King of Fighters '94
blurb: SNK's 1994 classic launched the 3-on-3 team battle system with 24 fighters against Rugal.
about: The King of Fighters '94 is SNK's Neo-Geo MVS fighting game released in August 1994, featuring 24 selectable characters in fixed teams of three battling to defeat Rugal Bernstein. It revolutionized the fighter genre with the introduction of 3-member team fighting called the team battle system, combining elements of Fatal Fury and Art of Fighting while bringing back characters from Ikari Warriors and Psycho Soldier. A new game in the series is produced every year.
