In the demo before the first Rugal encounter, Rugal shows statues he has gathered by turning opponents into them, including one resembling Capcom's Guile making a Sonic Boom.

title: The King of Fighters '95
blurb: SNK's 1995 sequel pits eight teams of three against Rugal, introducing rival Iori Yagami.
about: The King of Fighters '95 is SNK's Neo-Geo MVS fighting game, released on July 25, 1995 in Japanese arcades. Eight teams of three characters each square off again to take out Rugal Bernstein. The background for the Japan Team is a real place. Iori Yagami was introduced as Kyo's rival, a member of a rival martial arts school connected to the Ancient Arts of the Kusanagi, wielding red flames. His intense personality, unique moves, hairstyle, and provocative lines like 'You cry! You scream! Then you die!' broke the mold for fighting game characters at the time, and he stood out most during initial location tests.

title: The King of Fighters '96
blurb: The third KOF chapter unites 27 SNK characters against final boss Goenitz.
about: The King of Fighters '96 is SNK's Neo-Geo MVS fighting game released in July 1996, the third chapter in the series, bringing 27 classic SNK characters together against final boss Goenitz. It is the first game to include special phrases and poses when two particular characters fight, happening here only with Kyo vs. Iori, Terry vs. Geese, and Ralf Jones vs. Clark Steel. Cut moves found in the game code include Kyo's Saishuu Kessen Ougi 'Mu Shiki', Geese's Deadly Rave, and Choi's Hou'ou Kyaku, some of which debuted in later games. Leona entered the series as a replacement for Heidern, leader of the Ikari Team.

title: The King of Fighters '97
saveName: The King of Fighters '97: Global Match [Classic Edition]
blurb: Pick from 29 fighters and take down Orochi in SNK's 1997 Neo-Geo tag-team brawler.
about: SNK's 1997 Neo-Geo MVS fighter lets you build teams of three from nine squads plus two solo entries, bringing the roster to 29 fighters. The goal is to defeat the evil Orochi and those tainted by his blood. Yuri's Hien Rekkou special is a nod to Ken's Shoryuu Reppa, and the Kowloon backdrop hides cameos from Top Hunter and Art of Fighting 3. The names of Kyo, Iori and Chizuru echo the legend of the Great Serpent.
tips: Fights are three against three, and before the match you choose Advanced or Extra mode for your team.
Advanced mode stocks power gauge bars as you fight and lets you roll; Extra mode fills a single gauge, which you can charge by holding light punch, light kick and heavy punch.
The 1997 edition closes the Orochi story that began in The King of Fighters '95.

title: The King of Fighters 2000
blurb: SNK's 2000 fighter brings 34 characters and the Striker system against the formidable Zero.
about: The King of Fighters 2000 is SNK's Neo-Geo MVS fighting game released in July 2000, featuring 34 characters and the popular Striker assist system. Teams battle to defeat the mighty Zero and his bladed coat. Ramon was designed with South American audiences in mind, a masked Lucha Libre wrestler full of tricky body slams. Vanessa was conceived as a thirty-something woman who broke the mold of teenage female fighters, having first appeared as a Striker in the Dreamcast version of KOF '99 before officially joining KOF 2000 as a playable character.

title: The King of Fighters 2001
blurb: Eolith's 2001 KOF entry delivers 40 fighters and one of fighting games' hardest boss pairs.
about: The King of Fighters 2001 is a Neo-Geo MVS fighting game released in October 2001 by Eolith. With the largest KOF roster at the time totaling 40 characters, it delivers high-quality fighting action alongside one of the most difficult pairs of bosses in fighting game history. Ron, chief of the Flying Brigands, first appeared in KOF 2000's Benimaru Team ending, which earned first-rate reviews and became one of KOF's most popular episodes. He uses tricky Chinese boxing techniques and pursues a ghoulish goal of manipulating the dead, making his grand entrance in KOF 2001 as the boss characters' Striker.

title: The King of Fighters 2002
blurb: Playmore's 2002 fighter drops the Striker format and returns to classic 3-on-3 team battles.
about: The King of Fighters 2002 - Challenge to Ultimate Battle is a one-on-one fighting game for one or two players, developed by Eolith and released in October 2002 by Playmore Corp. It is the ninth game in the series. The game discarded the 4-on-4 Striker Match format of the previous three entries and returned to the 3-on-3 Battle format used before KOF '98, while revamping the Power Gauge system into a format similar to KOF '97's. Kusanagi was inserted into the game at the last moment due to demand for the return of the old Kyo, whose trademark black school uniform endures even though he is over 20.
tips: Fights are three against three: pick three fighters and the order they come in. When one is knocked out, the next steps in at full health.

The four Neo Geo buttons are light punch, light kick, heavy punch and heavy kick. Light punch and light kick together roll you past an attack, and heavy punch and heavy kick together do a blowback attack.
Press light kick and heavy punch together, with at least one stock in the power gauge, to enter MAX mode: for a short time you can cancel special moves into other special moves.

title: The King of Fighters 2003
blurb: SNK Playmore's 2003 KOF introduces the Tactical Leader System and Multi-Shift team battles.
about: The King of Fighters 2003 is an SNK Playmore Neo-Geo MVS fighting game released in November 2003. It offers 32 selectable fighters plus Evil Kusanagi, Chizuru and Maki Kagura, Adelheid Bernstein, and final boss Mukai. It was the latest entry in the series to run on Neo-Geo MVS hardware. Two new systems debut: the Tactical Leader System, which gives one team member favorable treatment in capability, and Multi-Shift, which lets players change characters freely during 3-on-3 battle. Ash Crimson was designed with the intent to create an attractive evil character.
tips: Your team of three can switch fighters in the middle of a round, not only between rounds.
One fighter is your team leader and gets a special Leader Desperation Move.

title: The Last Blade
blurb: SNK's 1997 weapons fighter pairs striking artwork with twelve blades and two bosses.
about: SNK's 1997 Neo-Geo MVS weapons-based fighter, known in Japan as Bakumatsu Rouman - Gekka no Kenshi, pairs beautiful artwork and sound with twelve selectable characters and two end bosses. Outside Japan it is called The Last Blade, and in Korea The Last Soldier. Released in Japan on December 5, 1997, it draws partly on the manga Rurouni Kenshin and is set during the Bakumatsu period (1860-1899). Its four avatar characters mirror the four gods of Japanese mythology.

title: The Last Blade 2
blurb: SNK's 1998 swordplay sequel delivers sixteen fighters and one final boss.
about: SNK's 1998 Neo-Geo MVS sequel, Bakumatsu Rouman Dai-ni Maku - Gekka no Kenshi, is a much-acclaimed swordplay fighter with sixteen selectable characters and one end boss. Outside Japan it is known as The Last Blade 2. Released in Japan on November 25, 1998, it includes homages to the legend behind Mulan and to Cantonese hero Wong Fei Hung. Akari and Juzoh serve as comedic relief, appearing beside the elephant depending on the matchup.

aka: Bakumatsu Roman: Dai Ni Maku Gekka no Kenshi

title: The Super Spy
blurb: SNK's 1990 Neo-Geo first-person beat-em-up with RPG elements, sending you into terrorist hideouts.
about: An SNK Neo-Geo MVS game released in October 1990, The Super Spy is a first-person beat-em-up with RPG elements in which players infiltrate terrorist hideouts and fight the bad guys. A few rooms hide a G-Mantle poster on the wall, a character later used as a striker in The King of Fighters 2000. Two players use an 8-way joystick with three buttons: A punches or uses a weapon, B kicks, and C chooses a weapon.

title: The Ultimate 11: SNK Football Championship
saveName: The Ultimate 101 Games For Windows XP
blurb: SNK's 1996 Neo-Geo soccer cart, known abroad as The Ultimate 11 - SNK Football Championship.
about: An SNK Neo-Geo MVS soccer game released in Japan in October 1996, titled Tokuten Oh - Honoo no Libero, which translates as 'Top Scorer - Flame of Libero'. Outside Japan it is known as The Ultimate 11 - SNK Football Championship. Two players use an 8-way joystick and three buttons that change function by situation: on offense A shoots or makes a low pass, B a high pass, and C a short pass, while on defense A slides, B plays rough, and C shifts the action player.

aka: The Ultimate 11: The SNK Football Championship

title: Thrash Rally
blurb: Pick your vehicle and race across snow, gravel, sand, and water in this top-down Neo-Geo rally game.
about: Thrash Rally is a top-down rally racing game from Alpha Denshi, released on November 8, 1991 for the Neo-Geo MVS. One or two players choose from vehicles with differing handling, acceleration, endurance, and top speed. World Rally Championship mode offers six rally cars across lap-based circuits with time limits. Paris-to-Dakar mode is a point-to-point race that also includes a buggy, motorbike, and truck. Tracks feature varied surfaces plus jumps, chicanes, and obstacles to avoid.

title: Top Hunter: Roddy & Cathy
blurb: Two bounty hunters battle galactic pirates across four elemental planets in this SNK Neo-Geo beat-em-up.
about: Top Hunter: Roddy & Cathy is a horizontally-scrolling beat-em-up released by SNK on May 18, 1994 for the Neo-Geo MVS. One or two players control Roddy and Cathy, bounty hunters tasked with stopping the Klaptons, galactic pirates threatening the cosmos. Players jump between foreground and background planes, and can extend their arms to grab items and enemies, or pull themselves onto ledges. The game borrows special moves from SNK fighting games like Fatal Fury and Art of Fighting, including Ko'ouken and shoryuken-style attacks. Pony Canyon/Scitron released a limited-edition soundtrack on July 21, 1994.

title: Twinkle Star Sprites
blurb: Cute versus shooting meets puzzle mayhem as Load Ran fights to save her world in this SNK Neo-Geo classic.
about: A competitive scrolling shooter from ADK, Twinkle Star Sprites blends fixed-shooter action with versus puzzle mechanics. Players chain shots and timed power-ups to damage their opponent, with attacks doubling as counters. It was ADK's final Neo-Geo production. Story Mode follows Load Ran and Rabbicat on their quest for the Magical Twinkle Star against the evil Mevious. Free Character Mode offers other fighters and unique comical endings, while a second player can jump in anytime.

title: Waku Waku 7
blurb: Sunsoft's 1996 Neo-Geo parody fighter packs seven selectable characters and a memorably nasty boss.
about: Waku Waku 7 is a 1996 Sunsoft arcade fighting game on SNK Neo-Geo MVS hardware, parodying anime and video game styles with seven selectable characters and a tough end boss. Released in November 1996, it supports two players with an 8-way joystick and four buttons. The bonus stage against Bonus Kun, a Shotokan punching bag, parodies Ryu and Ken from Street Fighter, and its music echoes Ryu's theme. Pony Canyon put out a limited soundtrack album (PCCB-00215) on 21/08/1996.

title: Windjammers
blurb: Data East's 1994 Neo-Geo flying disc game, known outside Japan as Windjammers, hits the arcade.
about: Flying Power Disc is a 1994 Data East Corp flying disc arcade game on SNK Neo-Geo MVS hardware, released February 17, 1994 in Japan and known elsewhere as Windjammers. Two players use an 8-way joystick and two buttons to slide, receive, throw, and lob. Each character speaks their own native language, and two mini-games appear: Dog Distance after match two and Flying Disc Bowling after match four. The game draws on the real sport 10-S, created in 1977 and copyrighted in 1980, without permission. On the USA territory dip switch, Korea's B. Yoo is swapped for Britain's S. Miller, keeping the same sprites but an English voice.

title: Zed Blade
blurb: Blast through space in this Neo-Geo shooter with three ships, swappable weapons, and a high-score table that bans 'AAA'.
about: Operation Ragnarok is a side-scrolling shoot-'em-up for one or two players on SNK's Neo-Geo MVS hardware, released by NMK in 1994. Players pick from three ships with different speeds, then configure front, rear, and projectile weapons such as Homing Missiles. Destroyed enemies and waves sometimes drop bonuses, weapon power-ups, and Hyper-Bombs, powerful smart bombs. Known as Zed Blade outside Japan, it hit Japanese arcades in September 1994 and never appeared on the Neo-Geo AES console. The high-score table refuses the initials 'AAA', changing them to 'YOU'.

title: Zupapa!
blurb: Guide a boxing-glove-wearing hero and his four Zooks through nine whimsical lands in this colorful Neo-Geo platformer.
about: Zupapa! is a whimsical action-platformer released by SNK for the Neo-Geo MVS in 2001. You control a long-eared, boxing-glove-wearing hero alongside four little sidekicks called Zooks, battling colorful enemies across worlds like Nightmare Land, Circus Land, Toy Land, and Dragon Land. Face first showed the game at the 1994 AOU Show, but it only saw official release years later, making it the only Neo-Geo unreleased prototype to eventually launch. It arrived months after Nightmare in the Dark, a game so similar that some players call it the adult counterpart to Zupapa's cute version.

title: 2020 Super Baseball
blurb: SNK's futuristic baseball sim lets you pick from 12 teams of men, women, and robots.
about: 2020 Super Baseball is SNK's Neo-Geo MVS take on the sport, set in a future where the Super Baseball Association has rigged games using a control computer. Players who discovered the manipulation removed the computer's connecting parts, leading to a fair match at 'CYBER EGG'. You choose from 12 teams mixing men, women, and robot players, with fast-paced rules and prizes earned from amazing catches that strengthen your squad. Two players can compete simultaneously with a CONTINUE mode. The game arrived in Japan on September 20, 1991, running on Neo-Geo MVS hardware with game ID NGM-030.

title: After Burner II
blurb: Sega's 1987 jet-fighter sequel puts you in an F14 Tomcat across 21 fast-moving stages.
about: After Burner II is Sega's 1987 arcade shooter built on the company's 3-D sprite-scaling technology, seating players in an F14 Tomcat. Across 21 colourful stages you gun down enemy fighters with an infinite-ammo machine gun and a limited stock of homing missiles, locking on before firing. Missiles are replenished every second stage via a support plane link-up or an automatic airstrip landing. Released in October 1987, it was once planned as a World War II-themed realistic flight sim before Yu Suzuki dropped that direction. Landing cut-scenes hide cameos: the Hang-On motorcyclist and the Out Run-style sports car. David Hernly set a record of 2,215,620 points on June 1, 2008, and an ABII unit…

title: Alien Storm
blurb: SEGA's 1990 arcade run-and-gun sends players against an alien invasion in a two-player world release.
about: Alien Storm is an arcade game released by SEGA Enterprises, Ltd in 1990. This is the two-player export (world) release, and the game was developed in Japan. It follows the original version, which was released as Model 317-0146. This edition carries Game ID 317-0154.

title: Altered Beast
blurb: SEGA's 1988 arcade beat-'em-up where heroes transform into mighty beasts to battle the underworld.
about: Altered Beast is an arcade action game released by SEGA Enterprises, Ltd in 1988. It is a Re-Edition of the original arcade version, which was released as Model 317-0066, while this edition carries Game ID 317-0078.

title: Art of Fighting
blurb: SNK's 1992 Neo-Geo fighter introduced the camera zoom and spirit meter to the martial arts genre.
about: Ryuuko no Ken is a martial arts fighting game released by SNK Corp in 1992 on Neo-Geo MVS hardware. One-player mode offers 2 selectable characters, while two-player mode offers 8, and a long-nosed boss awaits at the end. Progressive damage appears on each fighter's face. Launched in Japan in September 1992, its title translates as 'Dragon and Tiger Fist' and it is known overseas as Art of Fighting. It was SNK's second fighting-game franchise and the first fighting game to use a camera zoom and a spirit meter, with character designs by former SNK illustrator Shinkiro. Game ID: NGM-044.

title: Batman
blurb: Atari's 1990 arcade action game pits Batman against the Joker across Gotham City.
about: Batman is Atari Games' 1990 arcade action title in which the Dark Knight races to save Gotham City from the Joker. Alongside side-scrolling stages, it mixes in first-person Batmobile and Batwing sequences drawn from the movie. Released June 16, 1990 as a conversion kit priced at 1,095 USD, it shipped 500 kits in the United States and 101 in Ireland. Its digitized audio sampled Michael Keaton and Jack Nicholson, and a unit once belonged to Michael Jackson.

title: Battletoads
blurb: Three Battletoads brawl through six wild stages to stop the Dark Queen in this rare arcade-only beat-'em-up.
about: Battletoads is a mostly side-scrolling beat-'em-up for up to three players, who choose Rash, Pimple, or Zitz. Each Toad has a distinct fighting style — Rash is nimble, Pimple is burly, and Zitz balances the two — plus a signature attack that turns limbs into axes, drills, and more. The six stages mix 2.5D brawling with strictly 2D platforming, jet-pack tunnels, and a vehicle-shooting finale. Enemies include aliens, mutant rodents, and snowmen, and foes can be knocked off-screen toward the players. Released in December 1994 by Electronic Arts and licensed from Rare, it was never ported to consoles.

title: Bishoujo Senshi Sailor Moon
blurb: Banpresto's 1995 Sailor Moon arcade brawler sends the Sailor Senshi through five levels.
about: Pretty Soldier Sailormoon is a 1995 Banpresto arcade side-scrolling beat-em-up for one or two players, following the Sailor Senshi through five levels of anime-style combat. Players pick from five fighters who punch, kick, jump, and throw before facing each level's boss. Released on March 22, 1995 and developed by Gazelle, it uses magic crystals to fuel a screen-clearing special attack, much like Shinobi, and draws its moves from the Toei anime.

title: Buck Rogers: Planet of Zoom
blurb: Sega's 1982 cockpit arcade shooter sends Buck Rogers racing through a zooming alien gauntlet.
about: Buck Rogers - Planet of Zoom is a 1982 Sega arcade release, developed in Japan and offered in a cockpit model. It was published in December 1982 and also appeared as an upright model.

title: Captain America and the Avengers
blurb: Captain America, Iron Man, Vision, and Hawkeye battle Red Skull's forces in Data East's 1991 brawler.
about: Captain America and the Avengers is a 1991 Data East side-scrolling beat-'em-up with occasional shoot-'em-up sections. Players pick Captain America, Iron Man, Vision, or Hawkeye, each with a distinct weapon — shield, repulsor rays, solar beam, or bow and arrows — and allies like Quicksilver, Sub-Mariner, Wonder Man, and The Wasp appear to help. Foes include Klaw, The Living Laser, Whirlwind, The Grim Reaper, The Wizard, The Controllers, The Mandarin, The Juggernaut, Ultron, and Crossbones across five stages. Released in October 1991, it runs on Data East ARM6 hardware. Josh Bycer set the official record with 496,801 points on April 20, 1997.

title: Columns
blurb: Sega's 1990 falling-block puzzler drops three-block columns and rewards clever cascades over Tetris-style rotation.
about: Columns is Sega's 1990 answer to Tetris. A column of three stacked blocks drops from the top; players move it left or right but cannot rotate it. Instead, a button shifts the order of the colored blocks by one position. Matching three or more like-colored blocks horizontally, vertically, or diagonally clears them, and blocks above fall into the gap, often triggering cascades. Released in March 1990, it runs on Sega System C-2 hardware with 2 players, a 4-way joystick, and one rotate button. April Simmonds of Winnipeg, Manitoba, Canada, holds the official record with 267,360 points on November 13, 2006.

title: Congo Bongo
blurb: Sega's 1983 arcade favorite Congo Bongo appears here in its two-board version.
about: Congo Bongo is a 1983 Sega arcade release, developed in Japan. This entry covers the two-board version, SEGA ID 834-5180, using PCBs 834-5181 and 834-5167.

title: Contra
blurb: Grab a friend and battle Red Falcon's forces across ten stages in this classic run-and-gun arcade shooter.
about: In 2631, a meteor crashes into the Galuga archipelago near New Zealand, bringing a dormant alien with it. Two years later, the terrorist group Red Falcon seizes the island to launch an invasion of Earth, and Contra operatives Bill Rizer and Lance Bean are dispatched to stop them. This one or two player platform shooter spans 10 stages, mixing side-view action with 3D maze corridors inside enemy bases. Your semi-automatic machine gun has unlimited ammo, and you can move, jump and fire in eight directions at once. One hit kills you and costs you your current weapon.

title: Cyber Police ESWAT
blurb: Sega's 1989 arcade action game pits cyber police against the city's criminal underworld.
about: Cyber Police E-SWAT - The Ultimate Factor in the Battle Against Crime is a Sega arcade game from 1989. This export release was developed in Japan, where it debuted under the same title. The game carries the identifier 317-0130 and runs on Sega's arcade hardware of the era.

title: Double Dragon
blurb: Two brothers take on the streets in Taito's export release of the iconic beat-'em-up.
about: Double Dragon is a 1987 arcade game published by Taito Corp for releases outside Japan, under license from Technos Japan.
tips: Two players can fight together as Billy and Jimmy Lee.
The backward elbow is famously strong. Pick up the bats, whips, knives and barrels enemies drop.
In a two-player game, the brothers have to fight each other at the end to win Marian.

title: Double Dragon 3: The Rosetta Stone
blurb: Billy and Jimmy Lee chase the Rosetta Stone across the globe in the final arcade chapter of Double Dragon.
about: A fortune teller warns Billy and Jimmy Lee of a rising enemy in Egypt, and the brothers set out on a worldwide quest for the Rosetta Stone, picking up new allies along the way. This third and final arcade entry in the Double Dragon series swapped out the earlier gameplay and graphics for a new system, adding moves like the belly-to-back throw and back-to-back hurricane kick while dropping the hair grab and elbow punch. It was developed by East Technology rather than Technos' internal team, and supports up to three players, with the third controlling Sonny, a yellow-clad Lee brother unique to this game.

title: Double Dragon II: The Revenge
blurb: Billy and Jimmy Lee return to avenge Marian's death in this upgraded arcade beat-'em-up sequel.
about: After his defeat in the original Double Dragon, Black Warriors leader Willy strikes back by murdering Billy and Jimmy Lee's friend Marian, sending the brothers on a quest for revenge. The sequel keeps the original's attacks and combos while adding new moves like the invincible Cyclone Kick, plus redesigned stages, weapons and traps such as a bulldozer in Mission 3. Released in December 1988, the game swapped the usual punch and kick buttons for left and right attack controls. It began as a chip upgrade of the first game before growing into new hardware, and the coin-insert yell comes from the stick-wielding Mission 3 boss Chin Taimei.

title: Dragon Ball Z
blurb: Pick your favorite fighter from Akira Toriyama's manga and battle it out in this arcade adaptation.
about: Based on Akira Toriyama's famous manga, this 1993 Banpresto arcade game lets you play as many of the well-known characters from the show. It supports two players using an 8-way joystick and three buttons for punch, kick and hard attack. Released in November 1993, a limited-edition soundtrack album followed in 2005.

title: Fire Shark
blurb: Toaplan's 1989 vertical shooter soars into battle with relentless aerial action.
about: Fire Shark is a Toaplan arcade shoot'em up released in 1989, known in Japan as Same! Same! Same! This export version runs on Toaplan hardware under game ID TP-017. Romstar handled USA distribution and Dooyong handled Korean distribution. The Japanese original differs in that it allows only one player at a time, and after being hit you restart slightly behind where you left off.

title: Flicky
blurb: Guide Flicky the flightless bird as she rescues her lost chicks and dodges hungry house cats.
about: Flicky is a side-scrolling platform arcade game from Sega. Players control a flightless bird who must gather her scattered chicks, called chirps, and lead them to the exit door bearing her name. Cats emerging from cat-flaps roam the stages; contact costs a life, and any chick touched by a cat must be retrieved again. Each round is cleared by bringing all chirps to the exit. The first two rounds have six chirps, later rounds eight. Bonus rounds let Flicky catch falling chirps in a net for a Perfect bonus. The game was developed under the names Busty and Flipp before becoming Flicky, and released in May 1984 in Japan.

title: Forgotten Worlds
blurb: A Capcom arcade classic returns, bringing its distinctive run-and-gun action to a new generation.
about: Forgotten Worlds is an arcade release from Capcom USA, an updated version of the game originally published in Japan as Lost Worlds. It runs on CP System hardware, B-Board 88621B-2.

title: Frogger
blurb: Hop across busy roads and treacherous rivers to guide Frogger safely home.
about: Frogger is a one- or two-player arcade game from Konami. Players guide a green amphibian from the bottom of the screen to one of five home bases at the top, crossing five lanes of traffic and then a fast-flowing river filled with logs, crocodiles, and turtles that serve as platforms. Vehicle types move at different speeds, and some turtles dive underwater, drowning Frogger on contact. Konami released the game in Japan in June 1981, and it became a runaway hit. The coin-insert sound was later sampled by producer Richard X for the Sugababes' song 'Freak Like Me'.

title: Gain Ground
blurb: Rescue stranded troops and battle through fields and castles in this Sega shoot-em-up.
about: Gain Ground is a one- or two-player shoot-em-up released by Sega in 1988 on System 24 hardware. Each single-screen level challenges players to rescue lost troops before reaching the exit, choosing from three characters with unique weapons, strengths, and weaknesses. Time pressure means any troops left behind are lost, while rescued soldiers join as bonus players. Stages range across fields, castles, forests, and forts. The game arrived in Japan in November 1988. Cyber, one of the playable characters, was clearly influenced by the 1987 film RoboCop, and the final boss resembles ED-209 from the same movie.

title: Garou: Mark of the Wolves
blurb: Southtown hosts a new tournament as SNK's Fatal Fury saga enters its ninth chapter.
about: Garou: Mark of the Wolves is a one-on-one fighting game and the ninth entry in SNK's Fatal Fury series, released for the Neo-Geo MVS in November 1999. Set ten years after Geese Howard's death in a peaceful Second Southtown, it features 12 characters and drops the plane-switching battles of its predecessors for standard single-plane combat. The game introduced the Tactical Offense Position, a zone on the life gauge that grants a T.O.P. attack, gradual life recovery, and increased damage, plus the Just Defend system rewarding last-moment blocks. 'Garou' translates from Japanese as 'Hungry Wolf'.

title: Ghouls'n Ghosts
blurb: Capcom's ghoulish action classic brings its demon-filled quest to arcades outside Japan.
about: Ghouls'n Ghosts is an export arcade release from Capcom, developed in Japan and published in December 1988 outside the country. In Japan, the game is known as Daimakaimura. It runs on CP System hardware with B-Board 88620B-2.

title: Golden Axe
blurb: Three warriors storm Death Adder's realm in Sega's 1989 fantasy beat-em-up classic.
about: Golden Axe is Sega's 1989 side-scrolling beat-em-up set in a fantasy world where three heroes fight to rescue a kidnapped King and Queen from Death Adder. Choose Tyris Flare the Amazon, Ax Battler the Barbarian, or Gilius Thunderhead the Viking dwarf. Press jump and attack together for a special move, or double-tap left or right to charge. Knock a rider off a creature to mount it yourself, and hit Thieves to grab food and magic potions. The title screen's kanji reads 'Senpu', meaning 'Fighting Axe'.

title: Growl
blurb: Taito's 1991 arcade brawler Growl brings the fight to US shores as an export release.
about: Growl is the 1991 export version of Taito America Corp's arcade beat-em-up, released in the US in February 1991. It runs on the Taito F2 System hardware. For details about the game itself, see the original Japanese release, Runark. The title screen may read 1990, but the US release date was February 1991.

title: Hellfire
blurb: Taito's 1989 horizontal shooter lets you aim your fire in multiple directions.
about: Hellfire is Taito Corp's 1989 horizontal shoot-em-up, notable for letting players select their shooting direction. It arrived in Japanese arcades on April 20, 1989. An early version carried the title 'Captain Lancer'. Polystar put out a limited-edition soundtrack album for the game on June 25, 1989.

title: Hit the Ice
saveName: Hit the Ice: The Video Hockey League
blurb: No-holds-barred hockey hits the arcade with fights, brutal checks, and power drinks.
about: Hit the Ice - The Video Hockey League is Williams Electronics Games' 1990 arcade hockey title, built around the Reds versus Blues rivalry. Pass, shoot, and check opponents, each with their own bone-crushing style, and start fights to heat things up. An extra credit buys a 'power drink' that boosts speed and shot power for one minute at the start of a period. Released in December 1990 and developed by Taito Corp, the game appears in the 1991 film 'Terminator 2 - Judgment Day'.

title: Hook
blurb: The Lost Boys take on Captain Hook in Irem's 1992 arcade adaptation of the Robin Williams film.
about: Hook is Irem's 1992 arcade game drawn from the Peter Pan saga and the Robin Williams film, with the Never-Never Land children fighting to stop Captain Hook. It arrived in December 1992. All four Lost Boys appear, but only Rufio is named in the movie.

title: King & Balloon
blurb: Defend the king from balloon abductions in this classic 1980 arcade title.
about: This is the North American release of the 1980 arcade game King & Balloon, developed in Japan by Game Plan, Inc. The goal is to protect the king from balloons that try to carry him away. Released in the USA in December 1980, two months after the Japanese version, it featured redone voice samples. The king's cry for help was changed from a Japanese-accented 'Herupuu!' to a clearer English 'Help!'.

title: King of the Monsters
blurb: Smash cities and rivals in SNK's 1991 Neo-Geo monster brawler set in Japan.
about: SNK's 1991 Neo-Geo MVS release pits giant monsters against each other as they wreck a Japanese city. Think Rampage as a beat-'em-up: destroy the city while destroying your opponent. Released on February 25, 1991, it also received a limited-edition soundtrack album from Pony Canyon / Scitron on 21/09/1991.

title: King of the Monsters 2
blurb: SNK's 1992 monster sequel adds pesky small enemies alongside each stage's main foe.
about: This 1992 SNK Neo-Geo MVS sequel to King of the Monsters adds new elements, including small, annoying enemies on the battlefield in addition to the main foe in each stage. The MVS version was released on May 25, 1992.

aka: King of the Monsters 2: The Next Thing

title: Klax
blurb: Catch falling tiles and build lines of three in Atari's 1990 puzzle classic, Klax.
about: Klax is a 1990 arcade puzzle game from Atari Games. Players catch falling colored tiles on a paddle and flip them into bins to form lines of three or more, either horizontally, vertically, or diagonally. The goal is to complete waves without letting tiles fall into the pit. Though the title screen says 1989, it was released in February 1990. It was originally programmed in Amiga Basic by Dave Akers before being ported to C and running on hardware from Escape From the Planet of the Robot Monsters.

title: Mega Man: The Power Battle
blurb: Capcom's 1995 arcade fighter pits the Blue Bomber against a roster of Robot Masters.
about: Mega Man - The Power Battle is Capcom USA's 1995 North American arcade release, developed in Japan and running on CP System hardware. It is the arcade fighting spin on the classic Mega Man series.

title: Mercs
blurb: Capcom's 1990 arcade export Mercs brings explosive run-and-gun action to the CP System.
about: Mercs is a 1990 Capcom arcade export developed in Japan and running on CP System hardware with B-Board ID 89624B-3. It is the export counterpart to the Japanese release Senjou no Ookami II [B-Board 89625B-1].

title: Michael Jackson's Moonwalker
blurb: Guide Michael Jackson and his chimp Bubbles through isometric stages to rescue kids from Mr. Big's clutches.
about: Michael Jackson's MoonWalker is a 1990 Sega arcade scrolling isometric beat-'em-up based on the film, tasking Michael and his chimp Bubbles with saving children and toppling the evil Mr. Big. Players clear each round's henchmen and machines using charged magical energy shots or Dance Magic smart bombs, and touching Bubbles transforms Michael into the laser-and-missile-firing Moonwalker robot. Its five stages each carry a different Michael Jackson track, including 'Bad', 'Smooth Criminal', 'Beat It' and 'Another Part of Me', with 'Billie Jean' playing at the ending.
tips: Up to three players can play at once, each as Michael Jackson.
Rescue the kidnapped children in each stage. Your special dance attack clears the enemies on screen.
Catch Bubbles the chimp when he appears and Michael turns into a robot for a powerful stretch of the stage.

title: Mortal Kombat
blurb: Mortal Kombat's 1992 arcade debut brought digitized fighters, blood, and Fatalities to the world.
about: Mortal Kombat is Midway's 1992 one-on-one arcade fighting game and the first entry in the series, starring seven characters: Johnny Cage, Kano, Raiden, Liu Kang, Scorpion, Sub-Zero, and Sonya Blade. Battles use a best-of-three round format, drawing inspiration from Capcom's Street Fighter II for special moves and projectiles while introducing photo-realistic digitized fighters. After a win, a voice calls 'Finish Him/Her!' and the victor has seconds to perform a Fatality. Released October 8th, 1992 in the USA, it was renowned as the first fighting game to use digitized characters and blood, and was developed as a reaction to Street Fighter II with simpler controls. Its graphic violence…
tips: The original Mortal Kombat has seven fighters, with Goro as the sub-boss and Shang Tsung as the final opponent.
Block is a separate button, and down + high punch is the uppercut.
This game introduced the Fatality: a secret finishing move done after the "Finish him" announcement.

title: Mortal Kombat II
blurb: Mortal Kombat II expands the roster to 12 fighters and adds Babalities and Friendships.
about: Mortal Kombat II is Midway Mfg. Co.'s 1993 arcade sequel to the 1992 original, growing the character roster from 7 to 12 and improving the graphics. Matches are divided into rounds, with victory going to the first player to win two, and the losing fighter becomes dazed so the winner can attempt a finishing move. Standard moves were expanded: a crouching punch was added, the roundhouse kick is more powerful and knocks opponents across the screen, and hit box differences between high and low kicks are more marked. Returning characters gain new special moves, and MKII marks the first appearance of multiple Fatalities plus non-lethal finishers like Babalities and Friendships. Released in June…
tips: Block is a separate button; hold it to guard. Down + high punch is the uppercut, the most reliable anti-air in the game.
There are twelve playable fighters, with Kintaro as the sub-boss and Shao Kahn as the final opponent.
Mortal Kombat II added Babalities and Friendships to the Fatalities of the first game: each is a secret input done at the right distance after the "Finish him" announcement.

title: Ms. Pac-Man
blurb: Midway's 1982 maze sequel stars gaming's first female lead, with moving fruit, four maze layouts and the familiar ghosts.
about: Ms. Pac-Man is an arcade maze game released by Midway in 1982, the first proper sequel to Namco's pill-eating original. Players clear mazes of dots while dodging Blinky, Pinky, Inky and Sue, with four Power Pills in each maze. Ms. Pac-Man wears a bow and lipstick, and the bonus fruit moves randomly rather than sitting still. Four maze layouts rotate every two to four rounds. The game began as an enhancement kit called Crazy Otto by General Computing, and the name shifted from Mrs. Pac-Man to Miss Pac-Man before settling on Ms. Pac-Man.
tips: Ms. Pac-Man has four different mazes, and the bonus fruit moves around the maze instead of sitting still.
The ghosts are Blinky, Pinky, Inky and Sue, and they are less predictable than in Pac-Man.

title: NBA Jam Tournament Edition
blurb: Licensed NBA stars trade physics-defying dunks in wild two-on-two arcade basketball.
about: NBA Jam Tournament Edition is Midway's 1994 arcade basketball game for one or two players, built around two-on-two action with real licensed NBA teams and digitized players. An eight-way joystick and three buttons cover Shoot/Block, Pass/Steal and Turbo, with no fouls or free throws beyond goaltending and 24-second violations, letting players push and elbow freely as they leap far beyond human height for slam dunks. Each team carries three players and allows substitutions. It arrived on January 17, 1994 as a direct sequel to NBA Jam and an officially licensed NBA product.

title: Nemo
blurb: Capcom's 1990 arcade Nemo sends players into a dreamworld adventure on CP System hardware.
about: Nemo is a 1990 Capcom arcade game developed in Japan and released in export territories, running on CP System hardware. It shares its board lineage with the original Japanese release entry, Nemo [B-Board 89625B-1].

title: OutRun
blurb: Drive a red Ferrari Testarossa through Europe in Sega's legendary arcade racer.
about: Out Run is Sega's 1986 arcade racing landmark. You pilot a red Ferrari Testarossa across colourful European locations, dodging civilian traffic on twisting, hilly roads while racing each checkpoint's tight time limit. At every stage's end a fork in the road lets you choose your next route, and the in-car radio offers three tunes: 'Magical Sound Shower', 'Passing Breeze' and 'Splash Wave'. It launched internationally on September 20, 1986, and its deluxe cabinet came as a hydraulic tilting Ferrari Testarossa shell with speakers right behind the player's head.
tips: At each fork in the road you choose left or right, so a run takes you through five stages out of fifteen and ends at one of five goals.
Before the race you pick one of three songs for the car radio: Magical Sound Shower, Passing Breeze or Splash Wave.
Reach each checkpoint before the timer runs out. Shift down to low gear for a quick start and up to high gear for top speed.

title: Pac-Man (Arcade 1980)
blurb: The arcade icon that swallowed a generation, licensed by Midway for North America.
about: Pac-Man is Midway Mfg.'s 1980 export release of Namco's Japanese hit Puckman, brought to North America under license. Midway renamed the game and its hero, and gave the ghosts the nicknames Blinky, Pinky, Inky and Clyde. It launched in the USA on October 10, 1980, with 96,000 units produced in America. The game's early-'80s cult status even spawned Buckner and Garcia's single 'Pac-Man Fever', which reached #9 on the pop charts after its December 1981 release.
tips: Each ghost chases differently: Blinky follows Pac-Man directly, Pinky aims ahead of him, Inky's path depends on Blinky's position, and Clyde gives up the chase when he gets close.
Eating a power pellet turns the ghosts blue for a short time. Eat them in a row for 200, 400, 800 and 1,600 points.
A bonus fruit appears twice in each maze, just below the ghost house. The game famously breaks on level 256, where half the screen fills with garbage.

title: Pit-Fighter
blurb: Three digitized brawlers take on street thugs in Atari's crowd-brawling arcade fighter.
about: Pit-Fighter pits digitized fighters against a range of street thugs, with crowd interference and usable weapons adding chaos to the brawling. A Grudge Match mode lets players turn on each other. Released in August 1990 as a dedicated cabinet, it was one of the first fighting games with fully digitized protagonists, arriving two years before Mortal Kombat. The dedicated machine supported up to three players, while conversion kits typically went into two-player cabinets.

title: Puyo Puyo 2
blurb: Compile's 1994 puzzle sequel Puyo Puyo 2 brings the addictive falling-blob action back for two players.
about: Puyo Puyo 2 is a 1994 arcade puzzle game by Compile, the sequel to the hugely popular Puyo Puyo. It plays much like the original, matching falling blobs to clear them, and remains just as addictive and fun. The title screen reads 'Puyo Puyo Tsu' — 'Tsu' is a pun pronounced like 'Two'. It was licensed to Sega for manufacture and runs on Sega System C-2 hardware.

title: Rainbow Islands
blurb: Taito's 1987 Rainbow Islands casts Bub and Bob as humans building rainbows to scale each isle.
about: Rainbow Islands - The Story of Bubble Bobble 2 is a 1987 Taito arcade game, a sequel to Bubble Bobble. One or two players control Bub and Bob, restored to human form, who create solid rainbows used both as weapons and as temporary platforms while racing to the top of each island before time runs out. Released in October 1987, its fifth island, DOH Island, pays homage to Taito's Arkanoid, complete with Arkanoid-style enemies, block platforms and even its Game Over music. A bootleg called 'Jumping' appeared in 1989.

title: Rambo III
blurb: Taito's 1989 arcade shooter Rambo III sends you into Afghanistan to battle the Soviet army.
about: Rambo III is a 1989 Taito Corp arcade game where you take the role of Rambo and Colonel Sam Trautman fighting the Soviet army in Afghanistan. It runs on Taito B System hardware. Based on the film of the same name, it launched in Japan in May 1989 and in Europe that September. The movie is rated R by the MPAA, intended for mature audiences with parental guidance advised and no under-17s admitted without a parent or adult guardian.

title: Rolling Thunder 2
blurb: Namco's 1991 Rolling Thunder 2 returns agents to battle GERDRA with co-op play.
about: Rolling Thunder 2 is a 1991 Namco arcade scrolling platform shooter, continuing the 1986 original as secret agents fight the GERDRA organization. Doors hide enemies, weapons, and ammunition, and two players can now team up, with a female agent leading the solo role. Despite a 1990 title screen, the game arrived in March 1991. Victor Entertainment issued a limited soundtrack album on June 21, 1991.

title: Samurai Shodown
blurb: SNK's 1993 Samurai Shodown brought weapons-based dueling to the Neo-Geo.
about: Samurai Spirits, known outside Japan as Samurai Shodown, is a 1993 SNK Neo-Geo MVS weapons-based fighter with 12 characters, bonus rounds, and one end boss. Four buttons shift between armed and unarmed attacks. Released in Japan in July 1993, it pioneered weapon fighting in the genre using an upgraded scaling engine from Art of Fighting. Many characters draw on history, including Haohmaru, inspired by Miyamoto Musashi.

title: Samurai Shodown II
blurb: Fifteen weapon-wielding warriors clash in SNK's 1994 fighter that introduced the parry and POW meter.
about: Shin Samurai Spirits - Hahmaru Jigokuhen is a one-on-one fighting game from SNK, released in October 1994 on the Neo-Geo MVS. Fifteen weapon-wielding combatants battle to earn the right to face a powerful and difficult end boss. Building on the first game, SNK added characters and moves, including the POW meter for super specials that can break an opponent's weapon. It also introduced rolling, ducking, small hops, and the first offensive blocking technique, the parry. The game is known outside Japan as Samurai Shodown II.

title: Saturday Night Slam Masters
blurb: Capcom's 1993 wrestling brawler brings Muscle Bomber action to arcades outside Japan.
about: Saturday Night Slam Masters is Capcom's 1993 arcade wrestling game, developed in Japan and released internationally in July 1993. Japanese players know it as Muscle Bomber - The Body Explosion. Several wrestlers were renamed for audiences abroad, including Biff Slamkovich (Aleksey Zalazof), Gunloc (Lucky Colt), The Great Oni (Mysterious Budo), and El Stingray (El Stinger). The game runs on Capcom's CP System hardware.

title: SegaSonic the Hedgehog
blurb: Sonic, Ray, and Mighty race across Eggman Island in Sega's 1992 isometric arcade game for up to three players.
about: Segasonic The Hedgehog is a scrolling isometric racing game released by Sega, supporting one to three players as Sonic, Ray, and Mighty escape Eggman Island after Dr. Robotnik imprisons them in a tower. Gameplay keeps series staples like jumping on enemies and collecting golden rings, while levels are filled with lava flows, collapsible platforms, and locked gates. Though the title screen reads 1992, the game actually launched in Japan in September 1993, and it marked the first appearance of Ray and Mighty. It runs on Sega's System 32 hardware with a trackball and one button per player.
tips: SegaSonic the Hedgehog is not the Mega Drive game: it is Sega's 1992 isometric arcade game, built for a trackball, in which Sonic, Mighty and Ray escape Eggman Island.
Up to three players can run together. Each has an energy bar instead of lives; hits drain it and rings refill it.

title: Shadow Dancer
saveName: Shadow Dancer: The Secret of Shinobi
blurb: Sega's 1989 ninja sequel teams a shinobi with a loyal dog to defuse a terrorist bomb plot.
about: Shadow Dancer - Kage no Mai is Sega's 1989 arcade sequel to 1988's Shinobi. A young ninja and his canine partner hunt down time bombs planted across a metropolis by a terrorist group, fighting through jump-and-projectile action to stop the criminal mastermind. A key new move sends the dog at the nearest enemy by pulling down and pressing attack, pinning the foe until the player finishes them. If the dog is hurt it shrinks to a puppy and regrows after enough kills. The subtitle translates as Dance of Shadows.

title: Snow Bros.: Nick & Tom
blurb: Nick and Tom roll snowballs, trap monsters, and kick them flying in this cute 1990 Toaplan arcade classic.
about: Snow Bros. - Nick & Tom is a single-screen platform arcade game from Toaplan, released in April 1990. One or two players control snowmen Nick and Tom, throwing snowballs to encase enemies and then kicking the giant snowballs across the screen to destroy anything in their path. Across fifty levels, an invincible pumpkin head appears if you take too long, spawning unkillable ghosts. Defeated enemies may drop coloured potion power-ups, and the game was licensed to Romstar for USA distribution and ran on JAMMA-compatible hardware.

title: Space Harrier
blurb: Sega's 1985 sprite-scaling shooter sends a jetpack hero through a surreal 18-stage fantasy world.
about: Space Harrier is Sega's 1985 sprite-scaling shoot-em-up, set in the Fantasy Zone, a surreal landscape of abstract structures and checkerboard ground. The jetpack-carrying hero flies or runs while firing a laser at mammoths, alien pods, giant mushrooms, and a fireball-spitting Chinese Dragon boss. Across 18 stages, bosses wait at the end of nearly every one, with bonus stages at the 5th and 12th and a boss rush at the 18th. The game hit Japanese arcades in October 1985, and an early build had players piloting a spaceship instead of a flying man.

title: Star Wars
blurb: Atari's 1983 vector shooter puts you in Luke's X-Wing to fire a Proton Torpedo into the Death Star's exhaust port.
about: A single-player 3-D shoot-em-up from Atari, released in May 1983 and based on the first Star Wars film, Episode IV: A New Hope. Players are Luke Skywalker (Red Five), aiming to destroy the Death Star by firing a Proton Torpedo into an exposed exhaust port, surviving three attack phases first: a dogfight with Darth Vader and TIE Fighters, a run across the Death Star surface past laser turrets and towers, and the trench. The game engine came from a two-year-old space project called Warp-Speed, the controls were adapted from Battle Zone, and it was Atari's first game with speech, including Obi-Wan Kenobi's line 'The force will be with you--always'. 10,245 upright units sold at $2,295.

title: Street Fighter II: The World Warrior
saveName: Street Fighter II': Special Champion Edition
blurb: Capcom's 1991 arcade landmark Street Fighter II - The World Warrior, running on CP System hardware.
about: Street Fighter II - The World Warrior is an arcade fighting game published in 1991 by Capcom Company, Limited, running on CP System hardware. This entry covers a re-release on updated hardware. For details about the game itself, see the original Japanese release entry, Street Fighter II - The World Warrior [B-Board 90629B].
tips: This is the original Street Fighter II: eight fighters can be picked (Ryu, Ken, E. Honda, Chun-Li, Blanka, Zangief, Guile and Dhalsim), and the four bosses are computer-only.
Both players cannot pick the same fighter; that arrived in Champion Edition.
Between fights come bonus stages: wreck a car, then barrels and a pile of bricks, before time runs out.

title: Strider
blurb: Capcom's 1989 arcade action game, whose export title screen renders Strider in English over the burning Hiryu kanji.
about: A 1989 Capcom arcade game on CP System hardware, released overseas as an export version developed in Japan. On the export title screen, Strider appears in English above the 'Hiryu' kanji, which are colored with a purple gradient and start out red before catching fire, unlike the Japanese version where Strider is written in katakana to the left of the kanji. In the US version, Strider Hiryu is missing his yell when swinging his sword. The game was soon re-edited as Strider [B-Board 89624B-3].

title: Super Hang-On
blurb: Sega's 1987 superbike racer adds turbo boosts and four global courses to the Hang-On formula.
about: Super Hang-On is Sega's 1987 checkpoint-based racing sequel to Hang-On, which arrived two years earlier. Riders steer a superbike past rival bikers and roadside obstacles, reaching each stage's checkpoint before time runs out, across courses set in Africa, Asia, America, and Europe. Sega brought in the rolling roads seen in 1986's Out Run and added a turbo button. Holding turbo pushes the bike from its 280kph top speed to 324kph, a risky boost that is often needed to meet the game's tight time limits. It launched in April 1987.
tips: Choose one of four courses (Africa, Asia, America and Europe), from short to long.
Once you reach top speed, press the turbo button for a burst of extra speed.

title: Super Street Fighter II: The New Challengers
saveName: Super Street Fighter II: The New Challengers
blurb: Capcom's 1993 CPS-II fighter Super Street Fighter II: The New Challengers arrives in its export arcade release.
about: Super Street Fighter II - The New Challengers is a Capcom arcade fighting game released in 1993 on the CP System II hardware, developed in Japan and distributed as an export release on the Blue Board for USA and other territories. The export versions took localization liberties, altering Cammy's and Fei-Long's endings and changing some voice samples: Cammy's 'Spiral Arrow' became 'Cannon Drill' and 'Cannon Spike' became 'Thrust Kick', while Dee Jay's 'Slash' became 'Max Out'.

title: Superman
blurb: Taito's 1988 arcade brawler sends one or two Supermen across US cities to battle the Alien Powers.
about: A horizontal Taito arcade game released in December 1988 in North America and Europe, then February 1989 in Japan, playable by one or two players, with the second controlling a red Superman against the Alien Powers. Each player moves on foot or in flight with a joystick and uses two buttons to punch, kick, or fire Heat Vision, a high-intensity laser. Colored crystals grant extra energy and weapons such as the Super Blast Punch and Mass Terminator, and cars and gasoline cans can be picked up and hurled at enemies. Rounds take place in New York, San Francisco, Las Vegas, Washington, and an Alien Space Ship. The game opens with John Williams' brilliant musical score from 'Superman... The…

title: The King of Fighters '98
blurb: SNK's 1998 dream match brings 38 fighters and two fighting styles to the Neo-Geo.
about: This 1998 SNK one-on-one fighter offers 38 selectable characters and two play styles. Extra mode suits defensive players with a single power gauge, sidesteps and unlimited supers at low energy, while Advanced mode adds the evasive roll and up to three storable gauges. Released in Japan on July 23, 1998, it is known there as Dream Match Never Ends and is framed as Shingo's dream. Its soundtrack borrows themes from earlier KOF titles.

aka: The King of Fighters '98: The Slugfest
King of Fighters '98: Dream Match Never Ends

tips: The 1998 edition is a dream match with no story: fighters from every earlier King of Fighters game return.
Before the match you choose Advanced or Extra mode for your team, as in the 1997 edition.

title: The King of Fighters '99
blurb: SNK's 1999 Neo-Geo fighter debuts the striker system and expands teams to four characters.
about: SNK's 1999 Neo-Geo MVS entry introduces the striker system, expanding each team to four characters for a total of 30 selectable fighters. The goal is to defeat Krizalid and his evil feather coat. Released in Japan on July 22, 1999, it features a remixed Fatal Fury Wild Ambition theme for the Fatal Fury Team. K's original slicked-back hairstyle was changed, and Maxima began as a body-slam concept before becoming a fist-fighter.

aka: The King of Fighters '99: Millennium Battle

title: The New Zealand Story
blurb: Guide Tiki the Kiwi through eight-way scrolling stages to rescue his caged friends from a hungry leopard seal.
about: The New Zealand Story is an eight-way scrolling platform arcade game from Taito Corp, released in September 1988. Players control Tiki the Kiwi, who escapes the clutches of Wally, a large blue leopard seal, and sets out to free his kidnapped friends. Tiki starts with a bow and arrows but can pick up bombs, laser guns, and bouncing fireballs. Jump strength depends on how long the button is held, and players can commandeer balloons, blimps, and UFOs. Tiki also appears as a guest star in Taito's Liquid Kids and Bubble Symphony.

title: The Punisher
blurb: Capcom's 1993 arcade brawler puts you in the Punisher's boots, with an export version twist.
about: The Punisher is a 1993 Capcom arcade game, an export release of the Japanese original, built on CP System hardware. It's a side-scrolling beat-'em-up where you fight through enemies as the Punisher. One notable difference in export versions: the Super Kick produces blood graphics on enemies, replacing the blue flames seen in the Japanese release.
tips: Two players can team up as the Punisher and Nick Fury.
Your fighter draws a gun automatically when armed enemies come on screen, and grenades are limited, so use them on crowds.

title: Toki
blurb: TAD Corp's arcade export release from 1989, named after the son of the company's owner.
about: Toki is an arcade export release from TAD Corp, published in 1989. It was released in the USA on February 22, 1990. The export version was named after Toki, the son of TAD's owner. 1452 PCBs were available at launch, with 150 more added in March. The American version adds a 'Winners Don't Use Drugs' screen during attract mode.

title: Truxton
blurb: Pilot a lone fighter against an alien armada hiding inside five gargantuan asteroids.
about: Tatsujin is a vertical scrolling shooter released by Taito Corp on October 13, 1988. After surviving an attack on a cargo barge, players pilot a remaining fighter to repel an alien invasion and divert five asteroid fortresses. The game spans eight levels of non-stop action with five bosses. Its title translates from Japanese as 'Master', and it is known outside Japan as Truxton. Polystar released a limited-edition soundtrack album on June 25, 1989.

title: Twin Cobra
blurb: Taito's two-player export shooter from 1987, licensed to Romstar for US distribution.
about: Twin Cobra is an arcade export release from Taito Corp, published in October 1987. It was licensed to Romstar for US distribution in November 1987. Unlike the Japanese version Kyuukyoku Tiger, Twin Cobra supports two simultaneous players, stores three characters for high scores, and respawns killed players at their current position. Player 1's hero is red and player 2's is blue. These differences make Twin Cobra considerably easier than its Japanese counterpart.

title: Twin Hawk
blurb: Taito's 1989 export shooter with two-player action and respawning at your current position.
about: Twin Hawk is an arcade export release from Taito, published in June 1989 and developed in Japan. It is the export version of Dai Senpuu. Twin Hawk supports two simultaneous players, with purple and pink planes for players 1 and 2. When a player dies, they continue at their current position, compensated by tougher larger enemies and increased dynamic difficulty. Small orange bullets are harder to see than in the Japanese version.

title: Two Crude Dudes
blurb: Data East's 1990 arcade brawler hits North America with street-fighting attitude and two-player action.
about: Two Crude is the North American arcade release of Data East's Crude Buster, arriving in April 1990. It is a side-scrolling beat-'em-up for one or two players. For full gameplay details, refer to the original Crude Buster entry.

title: Ultimate Mortal Kombat 3
blurb: Midway's 1995 fighter expands Mortal Kombat 3 with new combatants and extra finishing moves.
about: Ultimate Mortal Kombat 3 is Midway's 1995 arcade update to Mortal Kombat 3, adding new characters to the original MK3 roster along with other additions and extras. Two players battle using an 8-way joystick and six buttons for punches, kicks, block, and run. Released in the USA on October 6, 1995, the game runs on Midway Wolf Unit hardware. A subtle detail: Rain's name in the demonstration uses a different font than the other fighters.
tips: Block is its own button, and Run is another: hold Run while walking forward to rush in, which drains the run meter under your health bar.
Most fighters have preset combo strings (press the buttons in the right order with good timing) that are hard to break once the first hit lands.
When your opponent hears "Finish him" or "Finish her", you can perform a finishing move: Fatalities, Animalities, Babalities, Friendships and Brutalities each need a specific input and distance.

title: Viewpoint
blurb: Sammy's isometric Neo-Geo shooter sends you through claustrophobic space corridors against swarms.
about: Viewpoint is Sammy's 1992 isometric shooter for SNK Neo-Geo MVS, the company's only game developed and released for that hardware. Players pilot a ship through futuristic, claustrophobic corridors armed with a chargeable pulse laser and three bombs: a scrolling wave of fire, a circular nova blast, and homing mini-missiles. Six stages await. Released in October 1992, it won Best Graphics and Best Music in a Cartridge Game at Electronic Gaming Monthly's 1992 awards. The opening cue "One, Two, Three, Four, Hit It!" was sampled from Kurtis Blow's "AJ Scratch.

title: Volfied
blurb: Taito's 1989 abstract shooter sends a lone pilot to reclaim his homeworld from alien invaders.
about: Volfied is Taito's 1989 abstract action shoot-'em-up and an update of the 1981 classic Qix. A space pilot returns to his homeworld of Volfied to find it under alien attack; the surviving inhabitants, hiding underground, signal him for help. Controlling a craft called The Monotros, the player moves along a rectangle's edges and holds the draw button to venture into unclaimed territory, creating closed shapes to capture areas. Each stage has one large enemy plus smaller foes; claimed sections trap and destroy smaller enemies inside for bonus points. Danger only comes while drawing a line.

title: Zero Wing
blurb: Toaplan's 1989 arcade shooter began as a training project for new hires before blasting into Japanese arcades.
about: Zero Wing is a 1989 arcade shoot-'em-up from Toaplan, released in Japan on October 20, 1989. It started as a non-commercial project to train Toaplan recruits, reusing the engine from Hellfire, before the team decided to release it. Staff from Hellfire and Truxton mixed with newcomers, and the soundtrack came from three composers with distinct styles.
